en: Chapter One:
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha! Having paid respectful homage to the Sugatas, together with their Sons and their Dharma-body, as well as all those worthy of veneration;
I shall explain, in brief and according to the scriptures, the entry into the vows of the sons of the Sugata.
Indeed, there is nothing new here to be said, nor do I possess skill in composition;
for this very reason, I have no thought for the benefit of others—this work of mine was done only to cultivate my own mind.
First, by this means, the surge of my faith to cultivate virtue increases;
furthermore, if another person of a nature similar to mine should see it, then for that reason as well, this [practice] is purposeful.
This attainment of the favorable moment is extremely difficult to find; it is the means for accomplishing the goals of human life.
If one does not contemplate what is beneficial now, how will such an opportunity ever come together again?
Just as in the thick darkness of night a flash of lightning momentarily reveals light, so too,
through the power of the Buddhas, the mind of the world may for a moment turn toward merit.
Therefore, virtue is always weak, while the power of evil is great and most terrible;
by what other virtue can that [evil] be conquered, were it not for the mind of complete enlightenment?
Having reflected upon many eons, the Lords of Sages have seen that this alone is beneficial;
for by means of happiness itself, happiness increases and carries across immeasurable multitudes of beings.
Those who wish to cross over the hundreds of sufferings of existence, those who wish to remove the calamities of sentient beings,
and those who wish to enjoy hundreds of manifold pleasures must never, indeed, ever abandon the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
The wretched one, bound by the prison of existence, is called a son of the Sugatas in an instant;
indeed, as soon as the thought of enlightenment has arisen, he becomes worthy of veneration by the worlds of men and gods.
Having taken this image of impurity, one fashions from it an image of the precious Victor, priceless;
therefore, take hold of that which is called the thought of awakening, which is exceedingly penetrating and most firm, like a potent medicinal elixir.

O you who are habituated to wandering through the cities of the various realms of existence, seize with firm resolve the jewel of the awakening mind (bodhicitta)— a treasure thoroughly examined by those of immeasurable wisdom and the world’s sole caravan leaders as being of great value.
Just as a plantain tree perishes after yielding its fruit, indeed all other forms of merit likewise go to ruin;
but the tree of the spirit of enlightenment (bodhicitta) constantly bears fruit, never perishes, and continues to produce [more].
Since one may cross over even the most terrible sins in an instant by taking refuge in him—
just as one escapes great dangers by relying on a hero— how is it that ignorant beings do not take refuge in him?
It consumes great sins in an instant, like the fire at the end of an eon;
its immeasurable benefits were proclaimed by the wise Lord Maitreya to Sudhana.
That bodhicitta should be understood, in brief, as being of two kinds:
the mind of aspiration for enlightenment and the mind of setting out for enlightenment. (Bca 1.15)
Just as a distinction is perceived between one who desires to go and one who is actually going,
so too should the wise understand the distinction between these two according to their respective order.
The mind of the vow for enlightenment yields great fruit even within saṃsāra;
however, it does not possess the uninterrupted continuity of merit that belongs to the mind of application.
From the moment he resolves his mind with an irreversible intention upon the liberation of the boundless realm of sentient beings, [he generates the spirit of enlightenment]. (Bca 1.18)
From that time forward, even while one is asleep or heedless,
streams of merit flow continuously and as boundlessly as the sky.
The Tathāgata himself stated this, along with its supporting arguments, in the *Subāhupṛcchā* for the sake of sentient beings who are inclined toward inferior [teachings]. (Bca 1.20)
Thinking, "I shall destroy the headaches of sentient beings," one whose intention is beneficial is embraced by immeasurable merit.
How much more so for one who desires to remove the immeasurable suffering of each [being], and who wishes to bring about for each one a being of immeasurable virtue? (Bca 1.22)
Whose mother or father will have such a wish for their welfare? Will it belong to the gods, the sages, or the brahmins? (Bca 1.23)
Even for those very same sentient beings, such a desire for their own sake has never arisen before, even in a dream; how then could it possibly arise for the sake of others?

How can this unprecedented and extraordinary jewel of a being be born—one in whom the intention for the welfare of others arises even where no concern for one's own self would otherwise occur? (Bca 1.25)
How indeed can the merit of the jewel of the mind be measured—that which is the seed of the world’s bliss and the medicine for the world’s suffering? (Bca 1.26)
The worship of the Buddha is distinguished even by the mere wish for their welfare;
how much more so by striving for the sake of all happiness for all sentient beings! (Bca 1.27)
Driven by the desire for escape from suffering, they rush headlong into suffering itself;
through delusion and the mere wish for happiness, they destroy their own well-being like an enemy. (Bca 1.28)

Whoever would bring satisfaction through former pleasures to those who are repeatedly tormented by the stage of suffering, and who would cut through all their pains— [that person is the best of beings]. (Bca 1.29)
He even destroys delusion; how could there be anyone equal to such a virtuous person?
Where is there such a friend, or where is there such merit?
Even one who returns a favor for a service rendered is praised;
what then can be said of a Bodhisattva, who acts as a benefactor even when unasked?

A donor who provides food for only a few people is honored by the world as a doer of merit, even if it is merely a momentary gift of a single meal, compared to one who provides sustenance for half a day while being subjected to contempt. (Bca 1.32)
How much more so for one who, throughout infinite time and for an infinite number of sentient beings,
grants [the gift] that is inexhaustible until the end of space and fulfills every desire?
Thus, the Lord has said that whoever harbors impurity in their own heart toward the Son of the Conqueror,
the master of the sacrificial session, shall dwell in the hells for as many eons as there are particles of that arising impurity.
Now, for one whose mind attains serenity, from that [serenity] a greater fruit shall arise;
for evil karma toward the Sons of the Conquerors requires great effort, whereas virtue arises without exertion.
I pay homage to their bodies, in which that supreme jewel of a mind has arisen;
I go for refuge to those mines of happiness, in whom even an injury results in a succession of bliss.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Praise of the Awakening Mind," in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
Chapter Two:
In order to correctly grasp that jewel of the mind, I now perform worship to the Tathāgatas.
And of the stainless jewel of the True Dharma, and of the sons of the Buddha, who are oceans of virtue.
As many flowers and fruits as there are, and whatever varieties of medicinal herbs exist;
as many jewels as there are in the world, and waters that are clear and delightful.
There are mountains made of jewels, as well as other forest regions delightful for their solitude,
with creepers radiant with the ornaments of flowers, and trees whose branches are bent down by excellent fruit.
And in the worlds of the gods and others, there are perfumes and incenses, wish-fulfilling trees, and trees made of jewels;
as well as lakes adorned with lotuses, whose sounds of swans are exceedingly enchanting.
And all these various kinds of crops grown without cultivation, or other objects of worship and adornment,
extending throughout the expanse of the realm of space— all these, too, are without ownership.
Having taken this with my intellect, I offer it to the preeminent sages together with their sons;
may they, who are most worthy of offerings and possess great compassion, accept it from me out of pity for me.
I am devoid of merit and greatly impoverished; I have nothing else for the sake of worship.
Therefore, O Protectors who contemplate the welfare of others, please accept this for my sake through your own power.
I give myself entirely and in every way to the Victors and likewise to their sons;
O Supreme Beings, please accept me as your own; through devotion, I enter into the state of servitude unto you.
Through being accepted by you, I shall be fearless in existence and work for the welfare of sentient beings;
I shall transcend my previous misdeeds and shall not commit further sin again.
In those fragrant bathing chambers, delightful with pillars radiant with jewels and canopies shimmering with pearls, their floors were made of clear, brilliant crystal.
With many jars made of great jewels, filled with pleasingly fragrant water and flowers,
I perform this bath for the Tathāgatas and their sons, accompanied by song and instrumental music.
I wipe their bodies with incomparable garments that have been thoroughly perfumed and cleansed of impurities;
thereafter, I give them excellent robes that are beautifully dyed and well-incensed.
With divine garments that are soft, smooth, and variegated in beauty, and with various excellent ornaments,
I shall adorn Samantabhadra, Ajita, Mañjughoṣa, Lokeśvara, and the others as well.

I anoint the bodies of all the lords of sages with the finest perfumes, whose scents spread throughout the entire triple-thousandfold world system; their bodies blaze with the luster of gold that is well-heated, highly polished, and perfectly cleansed.
With all fragrant and delightful flowers, such as the *mandārava*, blue lotus, and jasmine,
and with garlands that are pleasing to the sight, I worship the most worshipful lords of sages.
I incense them with clouds of smoke made delightful by abundant and shimmering fragrances;
and having offered various kinds of foods to be enjoyed, tasted, and drunk, I present them as an oblation.
I offer jewel lamps arranged in rows upon golden lotuses,
and I scatter delightful heaps of flowers upon courtyards smeared with fragrant paste.

I offer to those whose nature is loving-kindness clouds of celestial palaces, radiant ornaments for the face of every direction, beautified by long, hanging necklaces of pearls and gems, and made delightful by songs of praise.
I shall hold aloft these most beautiful jeweled parasols of the great sages, adorned with lovely golden handles and strung with pearls.
From now on, let delightful clouds of worship arise,
as well as clouds of musical instruments and song that bring joy to all sentient beings.
And upon all the jewels of the true Dharma, upon reliquaries, and upon images,
may rains of flowers, jewels, and other offerings fall continuously.
Just as Mañjughoṣa and others worship the Victors,
so do I worship the Tathāgatas, the Protectors, together with their Sons.
I praise those oceans of virtue with hymns that are like oceans of melodic branches;
may clouds of these songs of praise arise from them without end.
With prostrations as numerous as the atoms in all buddha-fields, I bow down to the Buddhas who have gone to every realm, together with their supreme assemblies of Dharma.
I pay homage to the shrines containing relics, as well as those that are the abodes of Bodhisattvas;
I offer salutations to my preceptors and likewise to other venerable ones.
I go for refuge to the Buddha until I reach the seat of enlightenment;
I go for refuge to the Dharma and likewise to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
With palms joined in reverence, I make this request to the perfectly awakened Buddhas who dwell in all directions, and also to the Bodhisattvas who possess great compassion.
In this beginningless saṃsāra, or even in this very life,
whatever evil I have committed or caused to be committed while like a beast;
And whatever I have rejoiced in for the sake of my own destruction out of delusion— that transgression I confess, tormented by remorse.
Whatever harm I have done to the Three Jewels, or to my mother and father,
or to other gurus and others, through the impulsive actions of body, speech, and mind;
O leaders, whatever terrible sin has been committed by me, a wicked person defiled by manifold faults, all of that I confess.
And how may I escape from this, O Leaders, for I am constantly filled with anxiety? May death not come to me before my accumulation of evil has been exhausted! (Bca 2.32)
And how may I escape from this? Save me quickly!
Let not death come too soon upon me while my sins remain unexhausted.
This death, which destroys all trust, does not examine what has been done or left undone;
it is untrustworthy to both the healthy and the sick, like a sudden, great thunderbolt.
"Because of the causes of the pleasant and the unpleasant, manifold evil has been committed;
that one must depart, leaving everything behind—this was not understood by me in such a way. (Bca 2.35)
Whatever object is experienced becomes a mere memory;
like everything experienced in a dream, once it has passed, it is never seen again.
Those who are unpleasant will not exist; those who are dear to me will not exist;
I myself will not exist, and everything will not exist.
While you remain right here, many loved ones and those not loved have already passed away;
yet the terrible evil committed for their sake remains standing before you.
Thus, I did not reflect that "I am a guest," and through delusion, attachment, and aversion, I have committed manifold evils. (Bca 2.39)
Day and night, without rest, the expenditure of life increases;
yet there is no further arrival of life—how then can I think, "I shall not die"?
Even here, while lying on my bed and surrounded by my kinsmen,
I must endure alone the agonies of the severing of my vital organs and other such pains.
When one is seized by the messengers of Yama, where is the kinsman? Where is the friend?
At that time, merit alone is protection; yet that was not cultivated by me.
"O Protectors, because I was attached to this impermanent life and did not recognize this danger,
I, being heedless, have accumulated much evil."
Even as he is led away today for the purpose of having his limbs severed, he becomes parched;
thirsty and with a wretched gaze, he perceives the world as something entirely different.
How much more so when one is presided over by the terrifying messengers of Yama,
seized by a fever of great terror, and overwhelmed by the discharge of excrement?
With fearful glances, seeking protection in the four directions, [he thinks]:
"Who will be a virtuous protector for me from this great terror?"
Seeing the directions empty of protection, I shall fall once more into confusion;
what then will I do in that place of great terror?
This very day, I go for refuge to the Lords of the World, who possess great power,
who are intent upon protecting the world, and who have conquered all fear.
And likewise, with my whole being, I go for refuge to the host of Bodhisattvas, who have realized the Dharma that destroys the fear of saṃsāra.
Overwhelmed by fear, I offer myself to Samastabhadra;
and once again, I offer myself by my own self to Mañjughoṣa.
And to that Lord Avalokita, whose conduct is agitated by compassion, I cry out with a cry of distress, terrified; may he protect me, a sinner.
Seeking protection, I call out with sincerity to the noble Ākāśagarbha and Kṣitigarbha, and to all those who possess great compassion. (Bca 2.52)
I pay homage to that Vajrin, at the mere sight of whom the wicked messengers of Yama and others flee in terror in the four directions.
Having transgressed your words, I now seek refuge in you out of fear; being terrified, quickly destroy my fear! (Bca 2.54)
Even one who fears a minor illness should not disregard the physician’s instructions;
how much more so when seized by the four hundred and four types of diseases?
For by even a single [fault], all the people residing in Jambudvīpa perish—
those for whom no remedy can be found in any direction.
In this matter, to think "I shall transgress the word of the omniscient physician who removes all thorns"—fie upon me, utterly deluded! (Bca 2.57)
I remain exceedingly vigilant even regarding other precipices;
how much more so, then, regarding a fall lasting for thousands of yojanas over a long period of time?
Thinking "death will not come this very day," it is not fitting for me to dwell in ease;
that hour will certainly arrive when I shall no longer exist.
"Who has granted me fearlessness? How shall I escape?
I shall certainly cease to exist; why then is my mind so well-composed? (Bca 2.60)
Of those things previously experienced and now lost, what essence remains for me, through my attachment to which I have transgressed the words of my gurus? (Bca 2.61)
Having abandoned this world of the living, as well as my kinsmen and acquaintances, I shall go somewhere all alone; what use have I for all these things, pleasant or unpleasant?
But this alone is the thought appropriate for me, always by day and night:
"Since suffering is certain to arise from the unwholesome, how may I escape from it?"
Whatever evil has been accumulated by me, foolish and deluded, whether it be naturally reprehensible or reprehensible by convention; Bca_2.64.
Standing before my lords with palms joined, terrified by suffering, and prostrating again and again, I confess all of that.
May the Leaders accept this transgression as a transgression;
O Protectors, this was not good, and it shall not be done by me again.
Thus ends the second chapter. Chapter Three:
May all the merit performed by all sentient beings serve as a respite from the suffering of the lower realms.
I rejoice with joy; may those who suffer dwell in happiness.
I rejoice in the liberation of embodied beings from the suffering of saṃsāra,
and I rejoice in the state of a bodhisattva and the state of a Buddha for the Protectors.
And I rejoice in the oceans of the generation of the mind [of awakening] of the Teachers, which bring happiness to all sentient beings and establish the welfare of all sentient beings.
With palms joined in reverence, I entreat all the perfectly awakened ones in every direction:
may they kindle the lamp of Dharma for those who, out of delusion, are falling into suffering.
With palms joined in reverence, I entreat the Victors who desire to enter nirvāṇa:
may they remain for infinite eons, lest this world fall into blindness.
Having performed all this in such a manner, by whatever merit I have acquired,
may I become the one who brings peace to all the sufferings of all sentient beings.
May I become medicine for the sick, and may I be their physician and their attendant as well, until they are free from disease forevermore.
May I destroy the suffering of hunger and thirst by raining down food and drink;
during the intermediate kalpas of famine, may I become food and drink myself.
May I become an inexhaustible treasure for sentient beings who are poor,
and may I stand before them in the form of various useful articles.
For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings, I relinquish without attachment my own bodies, as well as enjoyments and all merit acquired throughout the course of time.
Nirvana consists of the relinquishment of everything, and my mind seeks nirvana;
if I must relinquish everything, it is better that it be given to sentient beings.
I have made myself a source of happiness for all embodied beings; let them strike me, let them revile me constantly, or let them cover me with dust. (Bca 3.12)
Let them play with my body, laugh, and sport;
I have given my body to them—what need have I for this anxiety?
And let them perform whatever actions bring them happiness; may no misfortune ever befall anyone by relying upon me. (Bca 3.14)
For those whose minds become either angry or pleased by taking me as their object,
that very state shall be the cause for the perpetual accomplishment of all their aims.
Those who slander me, as well as others who do me harm, and even those who mock me—
may they all partake in enlightenment.
I am the protector of the protectorless, the caravan leader for those traveling on the road,
and for those desiring to reach the further shore, I am the boat, the bridge, and the causeway.
May I be a lamp for those seeking a lamp, a bed for those seeking a bed,
and a servant for all embodied beings who seek a servant.
May I become for embodied beings a wish-fulfilling gem, a jar of fortune, a perfected spell, a great medicine, a kalpa-tree, and a cow of plenty.
The elements, such as earth and the rest, serve as the various kinds of enjoyments for immeasurable beings dwelling throughout the entirety of space. (Bca 3.20)
Thus, for as long as the realm of sentient beings remains within the expanse of space, may I be the source of sustenance for them in manifold ways, until all have attained final liberation.
In the same way, I shall generate the mind of enlightenment for the welfare of the world;
and in that very same manner, I shall train in those precepts in their proper sequence.
Having thus taken up the thought of awakening with serene confidence, the wise one should further gladden the mind in this way for the sake of strengthening what has been undertaken: Bca_3.24.
Today my birth has become fruitful; I have well obtained this human existence.
Today I am born into the family of the Buddhas; I am now a son of the Buddha.
Likewise, I must now act as one who performs what is appropriate for my own family,
so that no stain shall fall upon this stainless lineage.
Just as a blind man might find a jewel among heaps of refuse,
so too has this bodhicitta somehow arisen within me.
This elixir has arisen for the destruction of death in the world;
it is an inexhaustible treasure-trove that pacifies the poverty of the world.
This is the supreme medicine that pacifies the diseases of the world;
for those weary from wandering on the path of existence, it is a tree of rest for the world.
The moon of the mind has arisen as a common bridge for all travelers to cross over the miserable realms, and as a cooling balm to pacify the heat of the world's afflictions.
It is the great sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance in the world;
it has arisen as the fresh butter produced from churning the milk of the true Dharma.
For this caravan of people traveling on the path of existence, who are hungry for the enjoyment of happiness,
this sacrificial feast of bliss has indeed arrived, providing satisfaction to all sentient beings who have come as guests.
Today I have invited the world to the state of a Sugata and to happiness in the interim;
indeed, before all the Protectors, may the gods, asuras, and others rejoice!
The third chapter, titled "The Embracing of the Awakening Mind," from the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
Chapter Four:
Having thus firmly embraced the awakening mind, the Son of the Conquerors—
One should always strive, without indolence, to avoid transgressing the trainings.
Regarding that which was undertaken impulsively or that which was not properly examined, it is even appropriate to make a vow such as, "I shall or shall not do this. (Bca 4.2)
That which has been investigated by the Buddhas and by their sons of great wisdom—why should I not also rely upon it to the best of my ability? (Bca 4.3)
If, having made such a vow, I were not to accomplish it through action,
what would be my destiny after deceiving them all?
It is said that even for a mere trifle, if a person, having thought of it in their mind, does not give it away again, they become a preta.
What will become of my destiny if, having loudly proclaimed with sincere devotion the unsurpassed bliss, I have deceived the entire world?
Only the Omniscient One understands this inconceivable course of action,
whereby even by relinquishing the thought of enlightenment, he nevertheless liberates those people.
For a bodhisattva, every transgression is thus particularly grave,
because by committing it, he causes the ruin of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, for anyone else who creates an obstacle to his merit even for a single moment—
that destroyer of the welfare of sentient beings— there will be no end to his miserable rebirths.
For by destroying the welfare of even a single sentient being, one is destroyed;
how much more so for all embodied beings dwelling as far as the limits of space?
Thus, wavering in saṃsāra due to the power of his downfalls and the power of the thought of awakening, one who has reached the [first] stage takes a long time [to progress].
Therefore, I must respectfully accomplish what I have vowed;
if I do not exert effort today, I shall go from the surface to the depths by means of the surface.
Immeasurable Buddhas, who seek the welfare of all sentient beings, have passed away;
yet, through my own fault, I have not come within the range of their healing power.
If even now I were to remain as I am, then again and again I would encounter miserable rebirths, disease, death, cutting, breaking, and so forth. (Bca 4.14)
"When shall I obtain such a rare thing as the appearance of a Tathāgata, faith, or even human birth, as well as the fitness for the practice of virtue? (Bca 4.15)
This day of health is free from affliction and accompanied by sustenance;
yet life is momentary and deceptive, and the body is like a borrowed object.
By conduct such as mine, human birth will not be obtained again;
when human birth is not obtained, how can there be virtue, since only evil prevails?
When, though worthy of virtue, I do not practice virtue,
being deluded by the sufferings of the miserable realms, what shall I do then?
For one who performs no virtuous deed and instead accumulates evil,
even the title "Sugata" will be lost for hundreds of millions of eons.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Human birth is extremely difficult to obtain;
it is like a turtle's neck entering the hole of a yoke in a vast ocean. (Bca 4.20)
From a single moment of committed sin, one will attain rebirth in Avīci for an eon;
what then can be said regarding the sins accumulated over beginningless time? How could there be a happy rebirth?
Nor is one liberated merely by experiencing that [suffering], for while experiencing it, one generates yet another evil. (Bca 4.22)
There is no greater deception than this, nor any greater delusion, that having obtained such a moment as this, I have not practiced what is wholesome. (Bca 4.23)
If, however, I reflect in this way and again sink down, deluded,
I shall grieve for a long time once more, driven by the messengers of Yama.
The unbearable fire of hell will burn my body for a long time;
the fire of remorse will certainly burn my mind for a long time as well. (Bca 4.25)
Having somehow reached this ground of benefit so difficult to find,
even though I know it, I am being led back once again to those very same hells.
In this matter I have no volition, as if deluded by spells;
I do not know by whom I am bewildered, nor who dwells within me. (Bca 4.27)
The enemies of craving, hatred, and so forth lack hands, feet, and other limbs;
they are neither brave nor wise—how then have I been enslaved by them? (Bca 4.28)
"Remaining well-established within my very mind, they strike me down;
yet even then I do not become angry—fie upon this endurance of what is unworthy! (Bca 4.29)
Even if all the gods and humans were to become my enemies,
they would not be capable of producing the fire of the Avīci hell.
When even the ashes of Mount Meru cannot be found due to its attachment [to the earth],
the powerful enemies that are the afflictions cast me there in an instant.
For even the very long lives of all other enemies do not equal this beginningless and endless, immense duration of my enemies, the afflictions.
When cultivated in accordance with their proper method, all things conduce to one's welfare;
yet these very afflictions, when indulged in, produce nothing but extreme suffering.
While these constant and long-standing enemies— the sole cause for the production of floods of calamities—
dwell within my heart, how could I possibly find fearlessness or delight in cyclic existence?
These guardians of the prison of existence are also executioners within the hells and other realms;
if I remain in the house of my own mind, within the cage of greed, how can there be happiness for me? (Bca 4.35)
Therefore, I shall not lay down my burden here as long as these enemies have not been slain before my very eyes;
for even when an offender is insignificant, those who are exalted by pride and firmly bound by their wrath do not go to sleep without having destroyed him. (Bca 4.36)
Fierce in their resolve to utterly destroy the darkness of those suffering from natural death at the forefront of battle,
they do not turn back until they have achieved their goal, disregarding the pain of being struck by arrows and spears.

How much less so for me, who am now intent on destroying the natural enemies that are the constant cause of all suffering— by what reason could I possibly feel dejection or despair today, even through hundreds of calamities?
Without any cause whatsoever, they bear the wounds inflicted by enemies upon their bodies like ornaments;
why then should sufferings be an obstacle to me, who am striving for the sake of a most precious accomplishment?

Fishermen, outcasts, farmers, and others whose minds are bound solely to their own livelihood endure the miseries of cold, heat, and so forth; why then should I not endure them for the sake of the welfare of the world? (Bca 4.40)
Having pledged to liberate the world from its afflictions as far as the limits of space in the ten directions, even this Great Being has not himself been liberated from those afflictions.
Speaking thus without knowing the measure of one's own strength would be like that of a madman;
therefore, I shall remain ever irreversible in the destruction of the afflictions.
In this regard, I shall become a grasper, harboring enmity and engaging in conflict—
except for that kind of affliction which follows from the destruction of afflictions.
Let my entrails gush out at will, and let my head indeed fall;
yet I shall by no means bow down before the enemies that are the afflictions.
Even if an enemy has been banished, he may still take up residence in another land;
however, such is not the case for the enemy of the afflictions, for once his power is fully restored, he returns. (Bca 4.45)
Where could that [affliction] go, residing as it does in the mind, having been cast out, so that by staying there it might strive for my destruction?
Effort is not for me alone, O dull-witted one; these wretched afflictions are to be overcome by wisdom and right view.

The afflictions do not reside in objects, nor in the collection of sense faculties, nor in between; they do not exist elsewhere than these. Where else, then, could they be situated that they thus torment the entire world? This is merely an illusion; therefore, release the terror in your heart and apply yourself to the exertion for the sake of wisdom. Why do you needlessly afflict yourself in the hells?
Having thus resolved, I shall exert effort for the sake of practicing the training as it has been taught;
for how can one who deviates from the physician's instruction attain health when the illness is to be cured by medicine? (Bca 4.48)
The Fourth Chapter: Training in the Bodhisattva Conduct from the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
Chapter Five:
One who wishes to guard the training must guard the mind with great effort.
The training cannot be guarded by one who does not guard the flickering mind.
Untamed rutting elephants do not cause such agony here as the elephant of the mind causes when it is unrestrained in the Avīci hell and other realms. (Bca 5.2)
If the elephant of the mind is bound on all sides with the rope of mindfulness, all fear has come to an end and complete well-being has arrived. (Bca 5.3)
Tigers, lions, elephants, bears, snakes, and all enemies;
all the guardians of hell, as well as dakinis and rakshasas—(Bca 5.4).
All these become bound by the binding of the single mind;
and all become tamed by the taming of the single mind.
For it has been stated by the Speaker of Reality that all fears and immeasurable sufferings arise from the mind alone.
By whom were the weapons in hell diligently fashioned?
By whom was the floor of glowing iron made, and from where did those women arise?
The Sage declared that all such things arise from a sinful mind;
therefore, there is nothing more terrifying in the three worlds than the mind.
If the perfection of generosity consisted in making the world free from poverty, then why is the world still poor today? How could that [perfection] have belonged to the Protectors of the past?

When there is the intention to renounce one's entire possession along with its fruit for the sake of all people, that is declared to be the perfection of generosity; therefore, it is indeed the mind itself.
"Where could fish and other creatures be taken so that I would not kill them?
When the mind of renunciation is attained, however, that is considered the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā). (Bca 5.11)
How many wicked people, who are like the sky, could I possibly kill?
For when the mind of anger is killed, all enemies are killed.
Where would there be enough leather to cover the entire earth? Yet, by means of just the leather of a single sandal, the whole world is covered. (Bca 5.13)
In the same way, external objects cannot be prevented by me;
I shall restrain my own mind—what is the use of restraining other things?
Even with both speech and body, that fruit is not obtained by one of dull conduct;
whereas even a single moment of a sharp mind can achieve such states as the nature of Brahman.
The All-Knowing One has declared that all recitations and ascetic practices, even those performed over a long period of time, are in vain if performed with a distracted or dull mind. (Bca 5.16)
Those by whom this secret mind—the entire essence of the Dharma—has not been cultivated, wander in vain through space to destroy suffering and attain happiness. (Bca 5.17)
Therefore, I must keep my own mind well-established and well-guarded;
apart from the vow of guarding the mind, what is the use of many other vows for me? (Bca 5.18)
Just as one standing among the fickle guards a wound with care,
so too should one standing among the wicked always guard the wound of the mind.
Fearing even a tiny bit of pain from a physical wound, one protects that wound with great care;
why then does one not protect the wound of the mind from being struck by the mountain of the aggregate [of suffering]?
For by dwelling in this state of mind, even among the wicked and even in the midst of women, the steadfast ascetic is not corrupted.
"Let my gains perish at will; let honor, body, and life perish; let everything else that is wholesome perish, but never my mind. (Bca 5.22)
To those who desire to guard the mind, I join my palms in reverence:
protect mindfulness and situational awareness with every effort. (Bca 5.23)
Just as a man overwhelmed by disease is incapable of all activities, so too a mind distracted by these two is incapable of all activities. (Bca 5.24)
For one whose mind lacks clear comprehension, that which has been heard, reflected upon,
and cultivated does not remain in memory, like water in a leaking jar.
Even many who are learned, faithful,
and devoted to effort may become defiled by transgressions due to the fault of lack of introspection.
Even after accumulating merits, those who have been robbed by the thief of non-introspection— which follows in the wake of the theft of mindfulness— go to an evil rebirth.
This host of thieves that are the afflictions seeks an opportunity for entry;
having found an opening, it robs and destroys the life of the good rebirths.
Therefore, mindfulness should never be removed from the gateway of the mind;
even if it has departed, it should be reinstated by recollecting the agony of the miserable realms.
For those fortunate ones who show respect even out of fear of their preceptor’s instruction,
mindfulness arises easily through living with the guru.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess unimpeded vision everywhere;
everything is indeed before them, and I stand before them.
Having reflected thus, one should remain in that state, endowed with shame, reverence, and fear;
in this way, the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) will arise for him again and again.
When mindfulness stands guard at the gateway of the mind for the sake of protection, clear comprehension arises and does not depart, nor does it depart once it has arrived. (Bca 5.33)
First of all, this mind must be constantly established in such a way that I should always remain like a piece of wood, as if devoid of sense faculties.
One should never cast about the eyes fruitlessly;
rather, the gaze should always be directed downward, as if constantly gazing inwardly.
One may occasionally look toward the directions for the sake of resting the gaze;
having seen a mere appearance, one should look back at it as a welcome.
At the beginning of the path and so forth, one should look repeatedly in the four directions to perceive danger;
having rested, one should look at the quarters, even turning back to look behind.
Whether advancing or retreating, having first examined what lies before and behind,
one should act after thus understanding the task at hand in all circumstances.
Having first resolved, "The body must be maintained in this way," one should then repeatedly observe how the body is positioned in the interim.
One should exert every effort to examine the wild elephant of the mind,
so that once it is bound to the great pillar of reflection on the Dharma, it shall not escape.
One should thus examine the mind, asking "Where does it dwell?",
so that one never abandons the yoke of meditative concentration for even a single moment.
If one is unable [to maintain discipline] due to circumstances such as fear or festivities, one may act according to one's ease;
for it has been stated that equanimity toward the precepts is permissible at the time of giving.
Having understood what one has begun to do, one should not think of anything else;
that very task should first be completed with an inner self absorbed in it.
For in this way all that is well-done is accomplished; otherwise, neither would come to pass.
Furthermore, the affliction of non-discernment will likewise continue to increase.
While various kinds of idle chatter proceed in many ways,
one should destroy the curiosity that has arisen regarding all such diversions.
Having remembered the training of the Tathāgata, one should immediately abandon even fruitless acts such as kneading clay, cutting grass, or drawing lines, out of fear.
When one desires to move about or wishes to speak,
one should first examine one's own mind and then act with fortitude and reason.
When one perceives that one's own mind is either attracted or repelled,
then one should neither act nor speak, but remain like a piece of wood.
When the mind becomes arrogant or mocking, filled with pride and intoxication, excessively sarcastic, crooked, and deceitful— [then one should subdue it]. (Bca 5.49)
Whenever there arises the semblance of self-exaltation, the disparagement of others,
or speech accompanied by insults and agitation, one should then remain like a piece of wood.
If my mind seeks gain, honor, or fame, or seeks a retinue, or seeks service for myself, then I shall remain like a piece of wood.
My mind desires to speak either harshly regarding the welfare of others, or for the sake of its own self-interest, or out of a desire for an audience; therefore, I remain like a log of wood.
Because [others] are impatient, lazy, fearful, arrogant, talkative,
or biased toward their own side, I therefore remain like a piece of wood.
Thus, observing that the mind is either afflicted or engaged in fruitless undertakings,
the hero should always firmly restrain it by means of its antidote.
It should be well-ascertained, very serene, steadfast, respectful and reverent,
modest, fearful, peaceful, and intent upon pleasing others.
This world is exhausted by childish desires that are mutually contradictory;
it is filled with compassion [for them], thinking, "For this [suffering] arises from their afflictions. (Bca 5.56)
Always under the control of myself and other beings regarding blameless things,
I maintain this mind like a magical creation, free from pride.
Recalling again and again this excellent opportunity obtained after so long,
I shall maintain such a mind as to be unshakable like Mount Sumeru.
Dragged here and there by vultures greedy for flesh, why does this body not act otherwise—why does it offer no resistance in this matter? (Bca 5.59)
Why do you protect this mind, having made it your own by identifying with this physical body?
If this [body] is indeed distinct from you, then what loss do you suffer in its destruction?
O fool, you do not accept a wooden statue as pure;
why then do you protect this putrid machine constructed from impurities?
First, by means of your own intellect alone, separate this skin-sack;
with the sword of wisdom, strip away the flesh from the skeleton.
Having even separated the bones, look at the marrow within;
investigate for yourself whether there is any essence here at all.
Having searched thus with effort, you have not found any essence here;
tell me now, why do you still protect this body?
You must not eat impurity, nor drink blood, nor suck on intestines; what will you do with this body?
It is appropriate to protect [the body] for the sake of food for vultures, jackals, and the like;
however, this little human body is merely an instrument for [one's] karma.
Even as you guard it in this way, merciless Death will snatch it away and give your body to the vultures; what then will you do?
Clothing and other such things are not given to a servant with the thought that he will remain forever;
since the body will depart after having consumed [your resources], why do you incur such expense?
Having given him his wages from that [work], now direct your mind toward your own welfare;
for not everything acquired by a wage-earner is returned to him.
Having conceived the idea of a boat regarding the body, and because its coming and going are determined by you,
make the body go wherever you wish for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
Thus, having brought oneself under control, one should always have a smiling face;
one should abandon the contraction of the brow into a frown, being the first to speak and a friend to the world.
One should not suddenly throw down chairs and such with a loud noise;
nor should one slam a door, for one should always delight in silence.
Moving silently and unobserved, like a heron, a cat, or a thief, one attains the desired goal; in this same manner, an ascetic should always conduct himself.
One should always receive with one's head the words of those who are skillful in exhorting others and who act to benefit them without being asked; thus, one should always be a disciple to all.
One should utter words of approval for all well-spoken words;
seeing one who performs meritorious deeds, one should gladden them with praises.
One should speak of virtues in one's absence and repeat them when others do so out of satisfaction;
and when one's own qualities are being discussed, one should cultivate the recognition of those virtues as belonging to others.
For all undertakings are for the sake of satisfaction, yet that is difficult to obtain even with riches;
therefore, I shall enjoy the happiness of contentment through qualities produced by the labor of others.
In this case, there is no expense for me whatsoever, and there will be great happiness in the next life;
whereas through hatred, there is the suffering of displeasure and great suffering in the world beyond.
One should speak with words that are placed with confidence, whose meaning is clear,
which are pleasing to the mind, pleasant to the ear, rooted in compassion, and uttered in a soft and gentle tone.
One should always look upon sentient beings with an upright gaze, as if drinking them in with one's eyes;
by relying solely on these, my Buddhahood shall come to pass.

Great merit arises from that which originates in constant application and firm resolve, as well as from that which arises through the cultivation of remedies; it also arises toward fields of benefit and virtue, and toward those who suffer.
One should always be endowed with diligence and be a self-reliant doer;
one must not grant anyone an opportunity in any of one's activities.
The perfections, beginning with generosity, become progressively more excellent;
one should not abandon a superior [virtue] for the sake of another, except in order to maintain the bridge of moral conduct.
Having understood this, one should always be diligent in the interests of others;
for a compassionate person who perceives the welfare of others, even what is prohibited is permitted.
Having shared [his food] with those who have fallen into misfortune, the helpless, and those established in vows,
he should eat a moderate amount and cast away the three robes outside.
One should not afflict this body, which is a servant of the true Dharma, for the sake of other things;
for in this very way, one may swiftly fulfill the hopes of sentient beings.
Therefore, one should not give up one's life as long as the disposition of compassion is impure;
however, when the disposition is equalized, that [life] may be sacrificed, for in this way one does not fall away.
One should not speak of the Dharma to someone who lacks respect, who is in a state of physical ease, or whose head is covered;
nor to one who holds a parasol, a staff, or a weapon, nor to one whose head is veiled.
One should not show profound and noble [teachings] to those who are small-minded, nor to women in the absence of a man;
one should practice equal reverence toward both inferior and superior dharmas.
One should not employ a recipient of the vast Dharma in a base teaching,
nor, having abandoned proper conduct, should one entice them with sūtras and mantras.
The discarding of tooth-sticks and saliva is not permitted;
it is undesirable in water or on land that is to be used [by others], and the discharge of urine and so forth is likewise censured.
One should not eat with the mouth full, nor with noise, nor with the mouth wide open; one should not sit with legs dangling, nor rub the arms together.
One should not share a vehicle, a bed, or a seat with another woman.
Having seen or heard anything that causes displeasure among the people, one should avoid it all.
One should not point at anything with a single finger, but rather respectfully with the entire right hand; one should indicate even the path in this manner.
One should not make any sound by waving one's arms even in a minor hurry;
rather, a snap of the fingers or the like should be made, otherwise one would be lacking in restraint.
One should lie down in the desired direction, like the Teacher when lying on his bed of final nirvāṇa;
being fully aware and mindful of rising easily, one must first certainly and necessarily [adopt this posture].
The conduct of Bodhisattvas is said to be immeasurable;
for now, one should certainly practice that conduct which purifies the mind.
Day and night, one should practice the three heaps at the three times;
by that, through reliance on the Bodhicitta and the Victors, all remaining downfalls are pacified.
Whatever states one may encounter, whether by one's own volition or under the power of another,
one should diligently train in those very instructions appropriate for each of those states.
For there is nothing whatsoever that is not to be learned by the sons of the Conquerors;
nor is there any merit that does not accrue to one who dwells in this manner.
One should act for the benefit of sentient beings either directly or indirectly, and never otherwise;
and for the sake of sentient beings alone, one should dedicate everything toward enlightenment.
One should never abandon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), even for the sake of one's life— namely,
one who upholds the bodhisattva vow and is skilled in the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
One should learn how to attend upon a guru from the *Śrīsaṃbhavavimokṣa*;
this and other such matters taught by the Buddha are to be understood from reading the *sūtras*.
The trainings are seen in the sūtras; therefore, one should recite the sūtras.
Furthermore, one should examine the root downfalls in the Ākāśagarbha Sūtra.
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* must certainly be consulted again and again, because correct conduct is demonstrated therein in detail. (Bca 5.105)
Alternatively, in brief, one should diligently study for now the *Sūtrasamuccaya* composed by the noble Nāgārjuna, and the second [work] as well.
Whatever one is restrained from, wherever, and for whatever reason—one should observe the training and practice accordingly for the sake of protecting the minds of worldly beings. (Bca 5.107)
This, in brief, is the definition of clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*):
the repeated examination of the state of one's body and mind. (Bca 5.108)
I shall practice with my body alone; what would be the use of verbal recitation? What will happen to a sick person by the mere recitation of a medical treatise? (Bca 5.109)
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, titled "Guarding Vigilant Awareness.
All this well-conducted conduct, generosity, and worship of the Sugatas—
That which has been accomplished over a thousand eons is destroyed by a single act of resentment.
There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to patience;
therefore, one should cultivate patience with effort through various methods.
When the thorn of hatred remains in the heart, the mind finds no peace, one does not enjoy joy or happiness, and one attains neither sleep nor steadfastness. (Bca 6.3)
Even those who rely upon him and honor him with wealth and respect desire to kill that master, for he is ill-favored by their hatred.
Even friends are distressed by him; he gives nothing and is not served.
In short, there is nothing by which one who is prone to anger remains well-established.
He who,
by perceiving anger as an enemy, destroys it through persistent effort, shall be happy both in this world and in the next.
Born from the occurrence of the undesirable and the obstruction of the desirable,
hatred— having obtained food in the form of mental distress— proudly destroys me.
Therefore, I shall deprive that enemy of his food,
for this foe has no purpose other than my destruction.
Even through the arrival of the most undesirable, my joy must not be disturbed;
for even in dejection there is no gain, whereas the wholesome is lost.
If there is indeed a remedy, what is the use of mental distress in that case?
But if there is no remedy, what is the use of mental distress in that case?
Suffering, humiliation, harshness, and ill-repute are undesirable for oneself or for those dear to one; for an enemy, it is the opposite of this.
Happiness is obtained only with great difficulty, while suffering remains constant;
since liberation comes through suffering alone, O mind, be firm!
The Durgāputrakas and Karṇāṭas endure in vain the pain of burning, cutting, and so forth for the sake of liberation; why then am I so cowardly?
There is no object whatsoever that is difficult for practice to accomplish;
therefore, by practicing with mild pain, even great pain can be endured.
Do you not see the purposelessness of the suffering caused by gadflies, mosquitoes, and gnats; the pain of hunger and thirst; and the great misery of severe itching and other ailments? (Bca 6.15)
One should not cultivate delicacy toward cold, heat, rain, wind, mental afflictions, diseases, imprisonment, and beatings; otherwise, suffering will only increase.
Some exert themselves especially upon seeing their own blood, while others fall into a swoon even upon seeing the blood of another. (Bca 6.17)
Since that [suffering] has arrived due to the mind's either rigidity or cowardice, one should therefore become difficult for suffering to conquer and should overcome the pain. (Bca 6.18)
Even in suffering, the wise person should not disturb the clarity of the mind;
for this is a battle with the afflictions, and pain is easily encountered in combat.
Those who, receiving blows from the enemy upon their own chests, conquer their foes—they alone are victorious heroes; all others are merely slayers of the dead.
Furthermore, another virtue of suffering is that through it, pride is cast off by means of spiritual urgency;
one feels compassion for those in cyclic existence, fear of evil, and a longing for the Victor.
I feel no anger even toward bile and other humors, though they cause great suffering;
why then should I be angry with sentient beings? For they too are provoked by conditions.
Just as this pain arises even though it is not desired,
so too does anger arise by force, even though it is not desired.
A person does not become angry by intending "I shall be angry," nor does anger arise with the prior thought "I will arise. (Bca 6.24)
Whatever offenses there may be, and whatever various evils, all exist through the power of conditions; indeed, nothing exists independently.
The collection of conditions has no intention, "I shall produce," nor does that which has been produced have the intention, "I have been produced. (Bca 6.26)
That which is indeed cherished as primary and that which is imagined to be the self— thinking "I am that very thing," one does not arise [with such a thought].
For that which has not yet arisen does not exist; who then would desire to become it?
Moreover, because it is occupied with sense objects, it does not even strive to cease.
For the self is eternal, insentient, and clearly inactive like space;
even when in contact with other conditions, what action can there be for that which is changeless? (Bca 6.29)
Since he was as before at the time of the action, what did he do for that action?
In the relationship "this is his action," what is the basis for that connection?
Thus, everything is under the control of another, and that [controller] too is powerless;
since all phenomena are thus motionless like magical illusions, at what can one be angry?
If it is asked, "Even prevention is not appropriate; for who prevents what?", [the reply is:
dependence is appropriate, because the cessation of suffering is intended.
Therefore, whether one sees an enemy or a friend acting unjustly, one should remain happy by reflecting: "Such are the conditions for this person."
If, however, accomplishment were achieved by one's own will for all embodied beings,
no one would experience suffering, for no one desires suffering.
Out of negligence, they harm themselves with thorns and the like;
out of anger, by depriving themselves of food and so forth; and out of a desire to obtain women and other such things that are difficult to attain.
Some destroy themselves by means of hanging or precipices, by consuming poison, unwholesome food, and the like, and through the performance of unmeritorious deeds.
When, being thus subject to the afflictions, they strike even their own dear selves,
how then could there be any restraint toward the bodies of others?
When these beings, maddened by the afflictions, are intent on destroying themselves, how can it be that not only is there no compassion, but anger even arises? (Bca 6.38)
If it is the very nature of fools to cause harm to others,
it is not fitting for me to feel anger toward them, just as it is not fitting to be angry with fire because of its inherent quality of burning.
Now, this fault is adventitious, while sentient beings are gentle by nature;
thus, their provocation is improper, like pungent smoke in the sky.
If, setting aside the primary object such as the staff, one becomes angry with the instigator,
then since he too was impelled by hatred, it is better that my hatred be directed toward hatred itself.
"In the past, I too inflicted such very same suffering upon sentient beings; therefore, it is entirely fitting that this [suffering] befall me, who caused harm to living beings. (Bca 6.42)
That weapon and my body—both are causes of suffering. Since I have taken up both the weapon and the body myself, at what should I be angry?
This boil in the form of a body has been grasped by me, blinded by craving; it is incapable of enduring being struck. Why, then, should I be angry at the pain therein? (Bca 6.44)
"I do not desire suffering, yet as a fool I desire the cause of suffering; since suffering has come about through my own transgressions, why am I angry with another? (Bca 6.45)
Just as the sword-leaf forest and the birds of hell are produced solely by my own karma, so too is this; at whom, then, should one be angry?
Impelled by my own karma, they have become my wrongdoers;
since they will go to the hells, have they not already been slain by me?
Relying upon these, my great evil is exhausted through my patience;
yet, by relying upon me, they go to hells of long-lasting suffering.
"I alone am the one who harms them, and they are my benefactors;
why, having inverted this truth, do you, with a wicked mind, become angry? (Bca 6.49)
"If my own mental disposition were virtuous, I would not go to the hells;
what concern of theirs is it here, if I have protected myself? (Bca 6.50)
If I were to retaliate, even then these beings would not be protected;
my own conduct would be impaired, and thus those poor wretches would be lost.
Because it is formless, the mind cannot be harmed by anyone anywhere;
yet, due to its attachment to the body, it is afflicted by bodily suffering.
This group consisting of insults, harsh words, and infamy does not afflict the body; therefore, why do you become angry in your mind?
If others have a lack of faith in me, how could that consume me,
whether in this life or in another, such that it would be undesirable to me?
If he is undesirable to me because he creates an obstacle to my gain,
then my gain will perish right here, but my evil will certainly remain.
It would be better for me to die this very day than to live a life of falsehood for a long time;
for even if I were to remain for a long duration, the suffering of death would still come to me at that same moment.
One who awakens after experiencing happiness for a hundred years in a dream,
and another who awakens after being happy for but a moment— [between these two, there is no difference in the nature of their experience].
Surely happiness ceases for both once they have awakened;
that very same analogy applies at the time of death between one who has lived long and one who has lived but a short while.
Even after obtaining many gains and enjoying pleasures for a long time,
I shall depart empty-handed and naked, like one who has been robbed.
If, while living for the sake of gain, I bring about the destruction of evil and the accumulation of merit,
surely for one who becomes angry for the sake of gain, there will be the destruction of merit and the increase of evil.
If that very purpose for which I live should perish,
what is the use of even such a life as that which accomplishes nothing but evil?
If you say that hatred toward one who speaks ill of others destroys living beings,
why does such anger not arise in you toward one who brings disgrace upon another?
Because their lack of faith depends on others, you should be patient with those who lack faith;
because the arising of afflictions depends on others, you should be patient with one who speaks ill of you.
Even toward those who destroy images, stupas, and the true Dharma, or who revile them, it is not fitting for me to feel hatred; for there is no affliction in the Buddhas and the like.
Seeing that the arising of [unwholesome] mental states occurs just as before when those who harm one's beloved teachers, blood relatives, and others, one should restrain one's anger.
The suffering of embodied beings is invariably caused by both sentient and insentient factors.
Since that suffering is seen to reside in the sentient being, therefore, forgive this suffering.
Some commit offenses out of delusion, while others, likewise deluded, become angry; whom among these actions do we call faultless, or whom do we call the offender? (Bca 6.67)
Why was this done previously, by which you are thus oppressed by others?
All are dependent upon their own karma; who am I here to act otherwise?
Having understood this, I shall likewise exert effort toward meritorious deeds,
so that all may come to possess hearts of mutual loving-kindness.
Just as when a house is burning, the fire, having moved to another house, might become attached to straw and such; it is then dragged out and removed.
Thus, when the mind is scorched by the fire of hatred due to attachment,
it must be abandoned at that very moment, for fear of the total incineration of one's merit.
If one who was destined for death was released after being cut asunder, what is wrong with that?
If one is released from the hells through human sufferings, what is wrong with that? (Bca 6.72)
If even this much suffering cannot be endured today,
why is anger— which is the cause of the torments of hell— not restrained?
For the sake of anger alone, I have been made to undergo this very same [suffering] in the hells thousands of times;
yet neither my own welfare nor the welfare of others has been accomplished by me.
And this suffering is not of such a kind as to fail to accomplish a great purpose;
therefore, for one who removes the suffering of the world, it is only appropriate to feel joy in this suffering.
If others have attained joy and happiness by praising one who is exalted by virtue,
why, O mind, do you not likewise rejoice upon praising him?
And this joy and happiness of yours is blameless and a source of well-being;
nor has this supreme means of winning over others been forbidden by those possessed of virtue.
If this [happiness] of yours were not dear to you as "his very happiness," then by ceasing to give wages and so forth, your benefit in both the seen and the unseen worlds would be destroyed.
When your own virtues are being praised, you desire even the happiness of others;
yet when the virtues of others are being praised, you do not desire even your own happiness.
Having generated the mind of enlightenment out of a desire for the happiness of all sentient beings,
why do you now become angry with those very beings when they obtain happiness on their own?
Why do you not desire for sentient beings that state of Buddhahood which is worshiped by the three worlds?
Seeing their fleeting honor, why are you so consumed with burning resentment?
He who nourishes those whom you ought to nourish gives to you alone;
yet, having obtained one who sustains your family, you do not rejoice, but instead become angry.
How could he not desire the welfare of sentient beings who desires their enlightenment? How can one who is angry at the prosperity of others possess the mind of awakening?
If that [gift] was not obtained by him because it remained in the house of the donor, in any case it does not belong to you; what is the use of that which has been given and then not taken?
What can merits do to prevent it? Or what can his own virtues do to him who is well-disposed? Tell me, how can you not be angry when he receives [benefits] but does not accept them? (Bca 6.85)
Not only do you fail to grieve for yourself for the evil you have committed,
but you also desire to compete with others who have performed meritorious deeds.
If something unpleasant has arisen for an enemy, what more could there be for your satisfaction?
It will not be without cause, even if it occurs merely through your wishing for it.
Therefore, since that [happiness] is established only by your own desire, what happiness do you have in their suffering?
Even if such a thing were to be beneficial, what could be a greater misfortune than this?
For this is a terrible hook cast by the fisherman of the afflictions;
because of it, the guardians of hell will purchase you and roast you in cauldrons.
Praise, fame, and honor lead neither to merit nor to long life;
they are of no use for strength, nor for health, nor even for the physical comfort of my body.
This much would be the self-interest of a wise person who understands his own interest:
that one desiring mental happiness should indulge in liquor, gambling, and the like. (Bca 6.91)
For the sake of fame, they squander their wealth and even bring about their own destruction.
Are syllables something to be eaten? And once dead, whose is that happiness?
Just as a child cries out in distress when a house of sand collapses,
so does my own mind appear to me when praise and fame are lost.
Since sound is devoid of mind, it is impossible for it to praise me;
rather, the cause of my joy is the thought that another person is indeed pleased with me.
What is the use of affection for another directed toward me?
For that pleasure of affection belongs to him alone; I do not receive even a small share from it.
If my happiness consists in the happiness of others, then let that happiness be mine everywhere;
why is it that I do not feel happy when others are made happy by the grace of someone else?
Therefore, the thought "I have been praised" gives rise to joy within oneself;
yet even in that case, because there is no such connection [between the praise and the self], it is merely the behavior of a child.
These things—praise and the like—destroy my equanimity and spiritual urgency;
they produce envy toward those with virtues and anger toward prosperity.
Therefore, those who have appeared before me to destroy my reputation and so forth are, in fact, engaged in protecting me from falling into the lower realms. (Bca 6.99)
For one who seeks liberation, this bond of gain and honor is improper;
how could I feel hatred toward those who liberate me from bondage? (Bca 6.100)
How can I feel hatred toward those who have become like door-bolts for one desiring to enter [the state beyond] suffering, as if by the very empowerment of the Buddha? (Bca 6.101)
"It is not right to feel anger here, thinking, 'He has created an obstacle to my merit.
Is there no austerity equal to patience? Surely this very opportunity for it has now presented itself."
Now, if I do not practice patience here due to my own faults, I have created an obstacle for myself when the cause of merit has presented itself. (Bca 6.103)
For that which does not exist without another, and which exists when that other is present—that alone is its cause; how can it be called an obstacle?
For it is not said that a petitioner who arrives at the proper time creates an obstacle to giving,
nor is it said that the arrival of one seeking ordination constitutes an obstacle to renunciation.
Beggars are easy to find in this world, but those who do harm are rare;
for no one offends me, since I am myself without offense.
Therefore, an enemy acquired through ascetic effort is like a treasure unearthed in one's own home;
because he is an aid to the practice of awakening, such an enemy is to be desired by me.
This fruit of patience was acquired by both me and him;
therefore, this should be given to him first, since patience was initiated by him.
If an enemy is not to be honored because he lacks the intention to achieve perfection through patience,
then how can the True Dharma be honored, even though it is the appropriate cause for achieving perfection?
If an enemy, who possesses the intention to cause harm, is not honored, how can I practice patience toward him? He is like a physician striving for my benefit.
Therefore, it is precisely by depending on that evil disposition that patience arises;
for this reason, that very person is the cause of my patience and should be honored by me like the True Dharma.
"Therefore, the Sage has declared that the field of sentient beings is the field of the Victors,
for by honoring these [beings], many have reached the further shore of prosperity."

Since the attainment of the Buddha-qualities from sentient beings and from the Victors is equal, what is the logic behind having such reverence for the Victors but not for sentient beings? (Bca 6.113)
The greatness of the intention is not inherent in itself, but rather arises from its effects;
since that greatness is equal [in all], sentient beings are therefore equal by virtue of it.
That one is worthy of worship because of a disposition of loving-kindness is simply the greatness of sentient beings;
that merit which arises from faith in the Buddha is simply the greatness of the Buddha. (Bca 6.115)
Insofar as they possess a portion of the Buddha's teachings, sentient beings are equal to the Victors;
however, no one is equal to the Buddhas in their infinite qualities, which are like oceans.
If even a minute quality of those who are the singular mass of the essence of virtues is seen anywhere, the three worlds are not sufficient for the purpose of honoring it.
However, a portion of the arising of the Buddha-qualities exists within sentient beings;
by acting in accordance with this portion, one performs worship of sentient beings.
Moreover, for those who are sincere friends and immeasurable benefactors, what other recompense could there be than the act of pleasing sentient beings? (Bca 6.119)

For the sake of those for whom [an act] done there would be a deed well-done—even if they pierce one's body and enter the Avīci hell—one should practice only every kind of goodness toward them, even if they are great wrongdoers. (Bca 6.120)

If even my own masters are indifferent toward their own selves for the sake of that [Dharma], how can I not show respect to those various masters and instead maintain a sense of servitude? (Bca 6.121)

Those in whose happiness the Lords of Sages find joy, and in whose suffering they enter into grief—for by pleasing them, all the Lords of Sages are pleased, and by harming them, harm is done to the Sages. (Bca 6.122)
Just as one whose body is ablaze finds no mental pleasure even through all desirable objects on every side,
likewise there is no means for those whose nature is compassion to find joy even when sentient beings are suffering.
Therefore, whatever suffering I have caused to those of great compassion by inflicting pain upon living beings, I now confess that sin; may those sages forgive me for having troubled them.
Today, for the sake of propitiating the Tathāgatas, I enter into servitude in this world with my whole being;
let the multitudes of people place their feet upon my head or trample me, so that the Lord of the World may be pleased.
This entire world has been made their own by those whose very nature is compassion; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, these beings who appear before us are those very Protectors themselves—why, then, show such disregard for them? (Bca 6.126)
This alone is the propitiation of the Tathāgatas; this alone is the accomplishment of one's own welfare;
this alone is the remover of the world's suffering; therefore, let this alone be my vow.
Just as a single king’s officer may oppress the great multitude, yet that far-sighted multitude is unable to retaliate against him. (Bca 6.128)
Since he is not alone, for his strength is the king's army,
he should not thus humiliate anyone who has committed an offense, however weak they may be.
Since the guardians of hell and compassionate beings alike derive their power from that [sentient being],
one should therefore serve sentient beings just as a servant serves a fierce king.
What could an angry king do that would cause the suffering of hell, which is experienced precisely through the mental distress caused by one's own cruelty toward sentient beings? (Bca 6.131)
What could a gratified king give that would be equal to Buddhahood—
that which is experienced through bringing joy to sentient beings?
Let alone the future Buddhahood that arises from pleasing sentient beings;
do you not see even in this very life the attainment of good fortune, fame, and well-being?
One who possesses patience, as they wander through cyclic existence, attains a pleasing appearance, health, joy, long life, and the abundant happiness of a universal monarch.

Thus, being patient, one should cultivate vigor, for awakening is established upon vigor. *The Sixth Chapter: The Perfection of Patience in the Bodhicaryāvatāra.* **Chapter Seven** Thus, being patient, one should cultivate vigor, for awakening is established upon vigor.
For without vigor there is no merit, just as there is no movement without wind.
What is vigor? It is enthusiasm for the wholesome. What is said to be its opposite?
Laziness, attachment to what is base, despondency, and self-contempt. (Bca 7.2)
Through a craving for reliance on sleep— the tasting of the pleasure of non-exertion—
and through a lack of revulsion toward the sufferings of saṃsāra, laziness arises.
Scented by the hunter that is the afflictions, you have entered the snare of birth;
even now, do you still not realize that you have come into the jaws of death?
Even as your own companions are being killed one after another before your very eyes,
you still fall asleep just like a buffalo belonging to a Caṇḍāla.
For one who is being watched by the Lord of Death and whose path is blocked on all sides, how can eating be pleasing to you?
How can sleep? How can pleasure?
Since death will soon arrive once its provisions have been fully gathered,
even if you were to cast off that laziness now, what would you do when it is too late?
"This has not yet been attained, this has been begun; this remains only half-finished"—thinking thus as sudden death arrives, "Alas! I am destroyed! (Bca 7.8).
Beholding his kinsmen, whose faces were swollen with the force of grief and whose eyes were red with tears, now rendered hopeless, as well as the faces of the messengers of Yama.
Tormented by the memory of your own sins, hearing the cries of those in hell,
and with your limbs smeared by screams of terror, what will you do in your utter confusion?
"It is only fitting that you feel fear here and now, like a living fish;
how much more so for one who has committed sins, facing the intense sufferings of hell! (Bca 7.11)
O delicate one, you suffer even when touched by warm water;
having committed deeds that lead to hell, how can you remain so at ease?
O you who desire results without effort, O delicate one subject to much suffering, O immortal-formed one seized by death—alas, you, miserable one, are being destroyed! (Bca 7.13)
Having obtained the boat of human birth, cross over the great river of suffering; O fool, this is no time for sleep, for such a boat will be difficult to find again.
Having abandoned the supreme delight in the Dharma, which is followed by an uninterrupted succession of joy,
how can you find pleasure in agitation, laughter, and the like, which are causes of suffering?
The power of non-despair, the array of strength, the subjection of the self to one's purpose, the equality of self and others, and indeed the exchange of self and others. (Bca 7.16)
One must not give way to despondency by thinking, "How can there be enlightenment for me?
because the Tathāgata, who speaks the truth, has declared this to be true.
They too were gadflies, mosquitoes, flies, and worms, yet by the power of their resolve, they attained the supreme enlightenment so difficult to reach. (Bca 7.18)
How much more so am I, a human by birth, capable of discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful;
why should I not attain enlightenment by never abandoning the principles of the Omniscient One?
Furthermore, I have the fear that I might have to give away my hands, feet, and so forth;
through lack of discernment, I would fall into confusion regarding what is of greater or lesser importance.
I shall be cut, split, burned, and even torn apart many times over for incalculable millions of eons, yet awakening will not come to pass.
But this suffering of mine, which is limited, is the means for attaining perfect enlightenment;
it is like the pain of an incision made to remove the agony of an embedded thorn.
All physicians bring about health through the hardships of medical treatment;
therefore, to destroy many sufferings, one must endure a small amount.
Even this appropriate treatment, the excellent physician did not prescribe; he treats those who are grievously ill with sweet and gentle care. (Bca 7.24)
At first, the Leader even enjoins one to the giving of vegetables and the like;
later, he gradually causes one to do that by which one would even give up one's own flesh. (Bca 7.25)
When wisdom arises toward one's own flesh as it does toward vegetables,
then what indeed is difficult for one who renounces both flesh and bone?
One is not suffering because one has abandoned evil; one is not dejected because of wisdom, since it is through false conceptualization in the mind that suffering arises in the body from evil.
Through merit the body is happy; through wisdom the mind is happy.
Remaining in saṃsāra for the sake of others, by what means would the compassionate one be distressed? (Bca 7.28)
Exhausting former misdeeds and receiving oceans of merit,
one proceeds more swiftly even than the Śrāvakas solely by the power of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Thus, proceeding from happiness to happiness, what conscious person would despair after having obtained the chariot of the awakening mind, which removes all weariness and fatigue? (Bca 7.30)
The power of desire, steadfastness, joy, and liberation exists for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings;
one should cultivate desire out of fear of suffering, while contemplating its benefits.
Having thus uprooted the opposing factors, one should strive to increase enthusiasm by means of the powers of zeal, self-respect, joy, renunciation, dedication, and mastery.
I must destroy the immeasurable faults of myself and others,
wherein even a single fault would not be exhausted even in oceans of aeons.
In this undertaking to exhaust the defects, not even a trace of mine is seen;
how is it that my chest does not burst asunder while bearing such immeasurable agony?
Many virtues are to be acquired by me for both myself and others;
the cultivation of even a single one of those virtues might not be possible within kalpas as numerous as the oceans.
Not even a trace of virtue have I ever practiced;
my birth, though somehow obtained and marvelous, has been spent in vain. (Bca 7.36)
I have not obtained the joy of the great festival of worshiping the Blessed One;
I have performed no service for the Teaching, nor have I fulfilled the hopes of the poor.
I have not granted fearlessness to those who were afraid, nor have I brought happiness to those who were suffering;
I have only become a thorn in my mother's womb for her own sorrow. (Bca 7.38)
Due to my previous lack of aspiration for the Dharma, such a misfortune has now befallen me; who then would ever abandon their aspiration for the Dharma? (Bca 7.39)
The Sage has declared that desire is the root of all wholesome qualities;
its root, in turn, is the constant cultivation of the fruit of karmic maturation.
Sufferings, mental distresses, various fears,
and the frustration of one's desires arise for those who commit evil deeds.
