Wherever the aspiration of those who perform virtuous deeds goes,
there it is honored by the value of its fruits through their merits.
But wherever the desire for happiness of an evildoer goes,
right there he is struck by the weapons of suffering born of those very evils.
Seated within the centers of vast, fragrant, and cool lotuses, their splendor nourished by the consumption of the sweet voice of the Jina;
their noble forms emerging from the lotuses awakened by the hand of the Sage, these sons of the Sugata arise before the Sugata through their virtuous deeds.
With all his luster stripped away by the messengers of Yama, crying out in agony, his body molten like poured copper by the heat of fire,
and his flesh torn away in pieces by hundreds of blows from flaming swords and spears, he falls repeatedly upon the intensely heated iron ground due to his own evil deeds.
Therefore, having cultivated such a virtuous aspiration with diligence,
one should practice it by undertaking the pride [of the deity] according to the ritual of Vajradhvaja.
Having first examined the necessary conditions, one should either begin or not begin;
indeed, it is better not to begin at all than to begin and then desist.
Even in another life that habit persists; moreover, suffering increases due to evil.
Furthermore, the time for action has passed, and that [goal] was not accomplished.
Pride should be applied to three things: actions, secondary afflictions, and capacities.
"This must be done by me alone"—this is pride regarding action (*karmamānitā*). *Bca* 7.49.
This world is independent of its afflictions and is incapable of accomplishing its own welfare;
therefore, I must act for their sake, so that I do not become like those people who are powerless.
Another performs a base deed while I am still present;
if it is out of pride that I do not do this, then let my pride perish—it is better for me that it should.
Having encountered even a dead lizard, even a crow acts like Garuḍa;
for even a slight misfortune afflicts my mind if it is weak.
Indeed, misfortunes are easily overcome by one who is rendered motionless by despair;
but for one who has risen up and is striving, they are difficult to conquer even for the great.
Therefore, with a firm mind, I shall overcome adversity with adversity; for one who has succumbed to adversity, the desire to conquer the three worlds becomes a mere joke.
For I must conquer all; I am not to be conquered by anyone.
I must bear this pride, for I am the son of the Lion of the Victors.
Those wretched beings who have conquered pride are not truly proud;
for one who is proud falls under the power of the enemy, and they have fallen under the power of the enemy that is pride.
Led to miserable rebirths by pride, even when born as humans they are deprived of joy; subsisting on the alms of others, they are slaves, fools, ill-favored, and emaciated. (Bca 7.57)
Even those ascetics who are despised by all and stiff with pride—
if they too are among the proud, tell me, what kind of people are the truly wretched?
They alone are proud and victorious, they alone are heroes, who carry pride for the sake of conquering the enemy that is pride;
those who, having struck down that foe of pride even while it is surging, bestow upon people at will the fruit of victory.
Though he may stand amidst thousands of arrogant ones belonging to the side of affliction, he is difficult for the hosts of defilements to overcome, just as a lion is by the herds of deer. (Bca 7.60)
For even in great hardships, the eye does not perceive taste;
likewise, even when encountering difficulty, one should not fall under the power of the afflictions.
Whatever action one happens to engage in,
one should become addicted to that very action, intoxicated by it, and insatiable in spirit, like one who desires the pleasure resulting from play.
Action is performed for the sake of happiness, yet happiness may or may not result;
however, for one for whom action itself is happiness, how can he be happy when free from action?
In cyclic existence, there is no satisfaction through sensual desires, which are like honey on the edge of a razor;
how then could there be satisfaction through the nectar of merit, which is auspicious and sweet in its ripening?
Therefore, even at the conclusion of an action, one should immerse oneself in that very action,
just as an elephant, scorched by the midday sun, first plunges into a lake.
But if there is a consequence of the loss of strength, one should abandon the undertaking;
and once it is well completed, one should let go of it through a desire for what comes next.
One should protect against the blows of the afflictions and strike firmly at the afflictions themselves,
like one engaged in sword-fighting with a skilled enemy.
Just as one who is afraid would quickly seize a sword that has fallen,
so too should one seize the sword of mindfulness when it has slipped away, while recollecting the hells.
Just as poison, having reached the blood, spreads throughout the body,
so too does a fault, having found a flaw, spread within the mind.
Just as one carrying a vessel of oil, guarded by men with swords in their hands,
would be intent on avoiding a stumble out of fear of death, so too should the practitioner of the vow be.
Therefore, just as one rises quickly when a snake has fallen into one's lap,
so too should one act with haste when drowsiness and laziness arise.
After having thoroughly repented for each individual transgression, one should reflect:
"How can I act so that this shall not happen to me again? (Bca 7.72)
For this reason, one should seek association or activity so that the practice of mindfulness may occur even in those circumstances. (Bca 7.73)
One should make oneself light by recollecting discourses on heedfulness,
so that one remains prepared in all circumstances, just as before, regarding the arrival of tasks and other duties.
Just as cotton wool is subject to the coming and going of the wind, so too should one come under the power of enthusiasm; in this way, spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) is fully accomplished.
The seventh chapter, titled "The Perfection of Vigor," in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
Having thus increased one's enthusiasm, one should establish the mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
But a person whose mind is distracted stands within the fangs of the afflictions.
Through physical and mental seclusion, distraction cannot arise;
therefore, having abandoned the world, one should avoid discursive thoughts.
The world is not abandoned because of affection, nor through craving for gain and the like;
therefore, in order to relinquish these, the wise person should contemplate as follows.

Knowing that one who is well-joined with insight through calm abiding effects the destruction of the afflictions, one should first seek calm abiding; and that is achieved through a delight that is independent of the world.
For whom could there be affection for things that are impermanent, when one shall not behold a loved one again for thousands of births? (Bca 8.5)
Not seeing [the truth], one falls into discontent and does not abide in meditative concentration;
even upon seeing it, one is not satisfied and is afflicted by thirst as before.
He does not see things as they truly are; through his agitation, he falls away from spiritual progress and is consumed by that grief and the longing for union with what is dear.
Through constant preoccupation with that [friend], one's short life passes away in vain again and again;
through an impermanent friend, the eternal Dharma is lost.
One who associates with fools will certainly go to a miserable rebirth;
one who does not desire such dissimilar association—what can be gained from the company of fools?
In one moment they become friends, and in another moment they become enemies;
ordinary people are difficult to please and become angry even when there is cause for satisfaction.
When addressed with what is beneficial, they become angry and restrain me from that which is wholesome;
yet if their words are not heeded, they, being enraged, go to an evil rebirth. (Bca 8.11)

Envy arises from one who is superior; rivalry from an equal; pride from one who is inferior; intoxication from praise; and resentment from blame—when, then, could any benefit ever come from a fool? (Bca 8.12)
Self-exaltation, disparagement of others, talk of delighting in cyclic existence—
such things are inevitably unwholesome, arising from the childishness of a fool.
Thus, for him as well, through association with that [world], there is the arrival of misfortune;
therefore, I shall dwell alone, happy and with an unafflicted mind.
One should flee far from the foolish; if one encounters them, one should propitiate them with pleasant words.
One should not, however, engage in continuous intimacy with them, but rather behave like a neutral, virtuous person.
Taking only the essence of the Dharma, like a bee taking honey from a flower,
I shall wander everywhere as if I were a stranger, unattached to anyone.
"I am successful, I am honored, and many desire me"—when such thoughts arise in a mortal, fear of death is born. (Bca 8.17)
Wherever the mind, deluded by pleasure, finds delight, that very thing,
having become a thousandfold suffering, stands before it.
Therefore, the wise person should not desire it, for from desire fear is born; this [suffering] passes away of its own accord—so, maintaining fortitude, one should wait.
Many became gainers and many became famous;
yet, along with their gains and fame, they were not known where they had gone.
Others despise me; why should I rejoice when praised? Others praise me; why should I despair when reviled? (Bca 8.21)
Sentient beings have diverse inclinations and cannot be satisfied even by the Victors;
how much less so by ignorant people like me? Therefore, what is the use of worrying about the world?
They revile the being who gains nothing and they look down upon the one who gains something;
how can delight arise from dwelling with those who are by nature a source of suffering?
The Tathāgatas have stated that a fool is not the friend of anyone,
because no affection arises in a fool except for his own self-interest.
The joy that arises through the gateway of one's own self-interest is merely joy for the sake of the self;
for it is like the agitation felt at the loss of wealth, since that agitation is caused by the loss of pleasure.
Trees do not harbor resentment, nor must they be propitiated with effort;
when shall I dwell together with those who are so pleasant to live with? (Bca 8.26)
Staying in an empty temple, at the foot of a tree, or in caves,
when will I go forth without concern, never looking back?
When shall I dwell, with my abode wherever I choose to roam, in these vast regions that are by nature free from the sense of "mine"?
Possessing only a clay bowl as my wealth, with robes that thieves cannot enjoy,
when shall I dwell without fear, no longer protecting this body?
When shall I go to my own natural place, the ground of the body, and compare my own body— subject to the law of decay— with other skeletons?
For this very body of mine will become so putrid that even jackals will not approach its vicinity because of its stench.
Even for this single body, the fragments of bone born together will go their separate ways;
how much more so, then, for other dear people?
A being is born alone, and indeed dies alone;
no one else shares in that suffering. What is the use of dear ones who only create obstacles?
Just as one who has set out on a journey takes up a dwelling along the way,
so too does the traveler through existence take up birth as a dwelling.
Before he is led away by four men and while he is still being mourned by the world, one should go to the forest at that very moment.
Through non-familiarity and non-opposition, being alone in this very body,
one who has already died to the world does not grieve when dying.
And no one moving nearby, even if grieving, causes him distress;
nor do any disturb his recollection of the Buddha and the other [objects of mindfulness].
Therefore, solitude— delightful, effortless, the source of auspiciousness,
and the pacifier of all distractions— should always be cultivated by me.
Freed from all other thoughts, with a mind one-pointedly focused on my own heart,
I shall strive for the concentration and the taming of the mind.
For sensual desires produce misfortune both in this world and in the next:
in this world through imprisonment, execution, and mutilation, and in the next through rebirth in the hells and other such realms.

For whose sake I have repeatedly joined my palms in supplication to male and female messengers, and for whose sake neither sin nor ill repute was previously taken into account— [for that very purpose, I shall now act]. (Bca 8.41)
I have cast myself into danger and squandered my wealth;
yet, it was by embracing these very things that I attained supreme bliss.
Why do you not attain peace by embracing at will those very same bones— neither other than these, nor belonging to anyone else, but entirely under your own control and free from possessiveness?
That face which was formerly seen— whether covered by a veil, or being lifted up with effort, or being lowered out of modesty— is now unseen.
Look! His face has now been made manifest by vultures, as if they could no longer endure the intense suffering [of his body]. Why do you flee now? (Bca 8.45)
That which was protected even from the falling glances of others has today been devoured; O envious one, why do you not protect it now?
Seeing this heap of flesh being devoured by vultures and other scavengers, [one realizes that] for others it is honored as food with garlands, sandalwood, and ornaments. (Bca 8.47)
You feel terror even at this motionless skeleton when it is thus beheld;
why then do you not feel fear when it is being moved by some *vetāḍa* demon? (Bca 8.48)
From a single morsel of food, both saliva and impurity are produced for these beings;
therein, impurity is undesirable to you, so how can the drinking of saliva be dear to you? (Bca 8.49)
Those possessed by desire do not delight in pillows that are soft to the touch with cotton stuffing, thinking, "It does not leak a foul odor," for they are deluded regarding impurity.
If there is passion even for that which is concealed, why would that which is unconcealed be unlovely?
If there is no purpose in it, why is the concealed part being crushed?
If you have no passion for the impure, why do you embrace another—
a cage of bones bound together by sinews and smeared with the mud of flesh?
Your own body is full of much impurity; therefore, maintain your resolve with that very thing. O consumer of excrement, forget this other bag of filth.
"You desire to see and touch it, thinking, 'I am fond of its flesh';
how can you desire this flesh which is by nature insentient? (Bca 8.54)
That mind which you desire to see cannot be seen, nor can it be touched; and that which can be touched does not know [itself]. Why then do you embrace it in vain?
It is not surprising that you do not perceive another's body as consisting of impurity;
it is truly astonishing that you do not recognize your own body as being likewise composed of impurity.
Having abandoned the young lotus, which blossoms at the rays of the sun free from clouds,
what pleasure can there be for a mind intoxicated by impurity within this cage of excrement?
If you do not wish to touch [the body] because it is smeared with impurities such as clay and the like,
why then do you wish to touch that which has emerged from the body?
If you have no passion for the impure, why do you embrace another?
That seed was produced from a field of filth and has been nourished by it.
Because it is small and born of impurity, you do not desire an unclean worm;
yet you desire this body, which is composed of much impurity and born from impurity.
O consumer of excrement, you do not feel disgust for your own impurity alone;
you even desire other vessels of filth.
Even the ground is considered impure when camphor and other pleasant things, or rice and condiments, have been spat out after being placed in the mouth. (Bca 8.62)
If you do not even resolve upon this impurity though it is directly perceived before you,
then look at other bodies as well, those fallen in the charnel ground, which are truly horrific.
Since great fear arises when the skin is torn away,
how can one, knowing this, again find pleasure in that very same thing?
Even though this fragrance is applied to the body, it comes from the sandalwood alone and not from anything else;
why then should one be attached to one thing because of a fragrance belonging to another?

If passion does not exist here because of the natural foulness [of the body], is it not true that there is no auspiciousness? Why then does the world, delighting in what is useless, smear it with perfume?
What does the body have to do with this? If sandalwood is fragrant, why is one attached to one thing because of the fragrance belonging to another? (Bca 8.67)
If the body— with long hair and nails, with teeth stained yellowish-white by grime, covered in filth and mud, naked, and naturally terrifying— [is thus], [then why do you not feel revulsion?]
Why is it being refined with such effort, like a weapon for self-destruction?
The earth is agitated by those who are mad and intent on deluding themselves.
Indeed, you feel revulsion upon seeing a few skeletons in the cemetery;
yet you take delight in a village-cemetery, crowded with moving skeletons.
And thus, even this impurity cannot be obtained without a price;
for its sake, there is the toil of acquisition and the suffering in the hells and other realms.
A child lacks the capacity for acquisition; how then could he be happy in youth?
Through acquisition one reaches youth, but once old, what can one do with desires?
Some, exhausted by their activities at the end of the day and possessed of base desires,
return home in the evening and lie down as if they were dead.
Others, distressed by the hardships of travel due to military expeditions,
do not see their wives and children even after many years, as they are intent on those goals.
That for which the self was sold by those deluded by desire has not been attained; instead, life has been spent in vain through the service of others.
For those who have sold their own selves and are constantly performing the bidding of others,
women give birth to them in forest thickets and similar places.
Fools, mocked by desire, enter into battle where life is in doubt for the sake of their lives; they even go into servitude for the sake of honor.
Some who are full of desire are being cut apart; others are seen impaled on stakes, being burned, or struck down with spears.
Understand that wealth brings endless misfortune through the sorrows of acquiring, guarding, and losing it;
for those whose minds are attached to riches and distracted by them, there is no opportunity for liberation from the suffering of existence.
Thus, for those possessed by desire, the disadvantages are many while the gratification is slight,
just like a draft animal pulling a cart that receives only a morsel of fodder.
For the sake of that mere fragment of taste, which is not difficult even for a beast to obtain,
this extremely rare perfection of the moment has been destroyed by one cursed by fate.
This exertion which has been made at all times for the sake of this body— which is inevitably perishable, insignificant, and destined to fall into hell and other lower realms— [is futile].
Therefore, even with a hundredth part of the effort required for that [bodhisattva practice], one may attain Buddhahood;
yet the suffering of the conduct [of a bodhisattva] is far greater than [the suffering of worldly beings], and that enlightenment is not for those possessed by desire.
Neither weapons, nor poison, nor fire, nor a precipice,
nor enemies can serve as a comparison for sensual desires, when one recalls the agonies of hell and other such realms.
Thus, having become weary of sensual desires, one should generate delight in solitude—
in the peaceful forest lands that are free from strife and fatigue.
On fortunate stone slabs, vast as palace terraces and cooled by the sandalwood-like rays of the moon,
fanned by the silent and gentle forest breezes, they walk to and fro and contemplate the welfare of others.
Having dwelt for as long as desired in empty houses, at the foot of trees, or in caves,
he wanders at will, freed from the weariness of protecting possessions and detached from expectations.
Dwelling wherever he pleases and dependent on no one,
the happiness of contentment that he enjoys is difficult even for Indra to attain.
Through such modes as these, by cultivating the qualities of seclusion,
one should, with discursive thoughts stilled, cultivate the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
First, one should cultivate equanimity toward oneself and others with such earnestness:
"All beings are equal in their suffering and happiness; therefore, I must protect them as I do myself. (Bca 8.90)

Just as this body, though manifold through its various parts such as the hands and so forth, must be protected as a single whole, so too is this entire world; though diverse, it is of one nature in its experience of suffering and happiness.
Even though my own suffering does not afflict other bodies,
nevertheless, that very suffering is unbearable for me because of my attachment to self.
Likewise, even if another's suffering is not perceived by me through my own self, nevertheless,
that suffering of theirs is unbearable to me because of my attachment to self.
I must destroy the suffering of others because it is suffering, just like my own suffering;
I must also benefit others because they are sentient beings, just like myself.
Since happiness is equally dear to me and to others, what is so special about myself that I should strive for my own happiness alone?
When fear and suffering are as unpleasant to me as they are to others,
what is so special about myself that I protect it and not another?
If it is not protected on the grounds that "I am not afflicted by their suffering," then why protect against the suffering of my future body, which does not afflict me now?
The notion that "I am that very same person even then" is false,
because one who has died is indeed different, and it is another who is born.
If it is held that whatever suffering belongs to someone must be protected by that very person, then why is the pain of the foot not protected by the hand? For it does not belong to the hand.
Even if this [practice] is improper, it proceeds from the ego-sense;
therefore, whatever is improper must be turned away, both one's own and that of others, according to one's strength.
The continuum and the collection are false, like a row or an army;
since that person for whom suffering exists does not exist, to whom will it belong?
All sufferings whatsoever are without an owner; because they are suffering, they must be warded off without distinction. What basis is there for restriction in this matter?

If it is asked why suffering must be averted, [the answer is] because there is no dispute among anyone that it should be so; and if it is to be averted, then all [suffering] should be averted, just as it is for oneself. If not, then [it should not be averted] for others either, just as it is for oneself.
If compassion causes great suffering, why does it arise with such force?
Having examined the suffering of the world, how could this suffering born of compassion be considered great?
If the suffering of many can be dispelled by the suffering of one,
then that suffering should certainly be produced out of compassion for both oneself and others.
Therefore, although Supuṣpacandra knew of the danger from the king, he did not eliminate his own suffering for the sake of removing the suffering of many others. (Bca 8.106)
Thus, those whose mental continuums have been cultivated in this way, for whom the suffering of others is as dear as their own,
plunge into the Avīci hell like swans into a lotus grove.
When sentient beings are being liberated, there arise those oceans of joy;
surely that alone is sufficient—what need is there for a liberation devoid of flavor?
Therefore, even after acting for the sake of others, there should be neither pride nor astonishment;
nor should there be a longing for the fruit of maturation, because of one's exclusive thirst for the welfare of others.
Therefore, just as I protect myself even from the slightest disparagement,
I shall likewise cultivate a mind of protection and a mind of compassion toward others.
Through habituation, the cognition "I" arises even toward the drops of semen and blood belonging to another, even though the object is unreal.
Likewise, why is another's body not grasped as "self"? For one's own body to be regarded as "other" is already established and is not difficult to achieve. (Bca 8.112)
Having recognized oneself as possessed of faults and others as oceans of virtues,
one should cultivate the relinquishing of one's own being and the taking up of that of others.
Just as hands and other limbs are accepted as being parts of the body, why are embodied beings not likewise accepted as parts of the world? (Bca 8.114)
Just as the notion of a self arises through habituation toward this body of ours, which is devoid of self, why does the sense of self not likewise arise toward others through habituation? (Bca 8.115)
Thus, even after performing the welfare of others, there is neither pride nor astonishment;
just as when one has fed oneself, no expectation for a reward arises.
Therefore, just as you wish to protect yourself from pain, grief, and the like,
so too should you practice a mind of protection and a mind of compassion toward the world.
Then the Protector Avalokita,
whose name is identical to his own, presided [over the assembly] in order to remove even the fear of timidity before the gathered multitude.
One should not turn back from difficult tasks because of the power of habituation;
for that very thing which causes fear upon hearing it, by that same thing one finds delight when not separated from it.
He who wishes to quickly protect both himself and others should practice the supreme secret: the exchange of self and other.
Since one feels fear even at the slightest danger due to excessive attachment to this self, who would not hate that self which brings fear like an enemy? (Bca 8.121)
He who, desiring to remedy his own dullness, hunger, thirst, and so forth, kills birds, fish, and deer, or stands as an ambush on the path; (Bca 8.122)
One who, for the sake of gain and honor, would even kill his own parents,
or seize the property of the Three Jewels, thereby becomes fuel for the Avīci hell.
What wise person would desire, protect, or worship that [self]?
One should not regard it as an enemy, nor should anyone honor it. (Bca 8.124)
"If I give, what shall I eat?"—this selfish concern is the state of a *piśāca* demon. "If I eat, what shall I give?"—this concern for others is the state of a king of gods (*devarāja*). (Bca 8.125)
Having oppressed another for one's own sake, one is cooked in the hells and other realms;
but by oppressing oneself for the sake of others, all perfections are attained.
By transferring that very desire for one's own exaltation— which leads to miserable rebirths, low status, and folly— to another, one attains a happy rebirth, honor, and wisdom.
By commanding others for one's own sake, one experiences servitude and the like;
but by commanding them for the sake of others, one experiences lordship and the like.
Whoever in the world is suffering, all do so out of a desire for their own happiness;
whoever in the world is happy, all do so out of a desire for the happiness of others.
What is the use of saying more? Behold this difference between the fool who seeks his own interest and the sage who acts for the sake of others.

Buddhahood is indeed not to be achieved; how, then, can there be happiness even in cyclic existence for one who does not effect an exchange of their own happiness for the suffering of others? (Bca 8.131)
Let alone the next world; even in this visible world, one's purpose is not accomplished:
for a servant who does not perform his work, and for a master who does not pay his wages.
Having abandoned the production of mutual happiness and the festival of happiness both seen and unseen,
deluded beings grasp at terrible suffering born from mutual infliction of pain.
Whatever calamities occur in the world, and however many sufferings and fears there may be—all these arise from the grasping at a self; so why do I grasp at this [body]? Bca 8.134.
Without abandoning the self, it is impossible to abandon suffering;
just as without abandoning fire, it is impossible to abandon burning. (Bca 8.135)
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying my own suffering and for the sake of pacifying the suffering of others,
I give myself to others and take others as myself.
O my mind, form the firm conviction: "I am connected with others. Having relinquished the welfare of all sentient beings, you must not think of anything else now.
It is not right for one's own eyes and other faculties to perceive their own objects;
it is likewise not right for the hands and other limbs belonging to another to exert themselves for one's own sake.
Therefore, being devoted to the welfare of sentient beings, whatever you perceive within this body,
take that very thing away from it and act for the benefit of others.
Having conceived of yourself as being among those who are inferior and so forth, and likewise conceiving of others as being yourself,
you should cultivate envy and pride with a mind free from conceptual construction.
"This person is honored, but I am not; he is a recipient of gain, but I am not like him.
This one is praised, while I am censured; I am miserable, while this one is happy. (Bca 8.141)
"I perform actions, while he remains well-established;
he is indeed great in the world, while I am indeed base and devoid of merit. (Bca 8.142)
What can be done by one who is devoid of virtue, for the Self of everyone is endowed with virtues?
There are those among whom I am base, and there are those among whom I am excellent. (Bca 8.143)

I am to be treated according to my capacity by the power of the afflictions, such as the failure of morality and views, and not by my own will; even suffering has been accepted by me for that purpose.
"Now, since I am incurable for him, why does he despise me? What use have I for his virtues; rather, it is this person who possesses virtues. (Bca 8.145)
While standing in the jaws of the beasts of prey of the miserable realms, he feels no compassion for living beings;
instead, out of pride in his own virtues, he seeks to conquer other wise men.
Since one must observe oneself as being equal [to others] in order to increase one's own excellence,
one should strive to secure for oneself gain and honor, even by means of a quarrel.
May my virtues become manifest throughout the entire world;
yet, may there be some who do not even hear of his virtues.
"May my faults be concealed; may I receive honor and not he.
Today my gains are well-acquired; I am honored, but he is not. (Bca 8.149)
Let us watch with joy for a long time this man who has been humiliated, made an object of laughter for all people, and reviled here and there. (Bca 8.150)
For even this wretched fellow, it is said, competes with me;
yet what learning, wisdom, appearance, lineage, or wealth does he possess? (Bca 8.151)
Having thus heard my own virtues being proclaimed here and there, with my hair standing on end and filled with joy, I shall enjoy this festival of happiness. (Bca 8.152)
Even if he should obtain some gain, we should take it from him by force,
provided that after giving him just enough for his sustenance, he performs our work.
This one must be made to fall from happiness and always be joined with our own suffering;
by means of him, we have all been tormented by the pains of cyclic existence hundreds of times.
Immeasurable eons have passed while you have sought to know your own self-interest;
through this great exertion, you have only accumulated suffering.
Therefore, at my request, proceed here also without hesitation;
you shall see these benefits later, for the word of the Sage is indeed true.
If this karma had been performed by you in the past, then,
setting aside the bliss of the Buddha's perfection, this present state would not have come to pass.
Therefore, just as you have conceived an ego-sense toward drops of semen and blood belonging to others, so too should you cultivate that same sense toward other things.
Becoming a spy for others, whatever you perceive within this body, take that very thing away for their sake and act for the benefit of others. (Bca 8.159)
"This one is well-off while that one is miserable; this one is lowly while that one is high;
that one does something while this one does not"—do not harbor such envy within yourself. (Bca 8.160)
Deprive yourself of happiness and subject yourself to the suffering of others;
investigate his every move with the intent, "When will he do what? What is he doing?"—thus scrutinize him for faults.
Cast even a fault committed by another upon his very head;
and reveal even the slightest fault of this great sage.
Defile his reputation with talk of the superior fame of others,
and make him carry out tasks for sentient beings like a lowly slave.
For this person is composed of faults; he is not to be praised for any adventitious qualities.
Act in such a way that no one may perceive his virtue.
In brief, whatever harm you have done to others for your own sake,
turn that very same suffering upon yourself for the sake of sentient beings.
One should not give him any encouragement that would make him talkative;
rather, he should be established in the conduct of a new bride—modest, fearful, and restrained.
"Do this; remain thus; this must not be done by you.
In this way he is to be brought under control, and he is to be restrained when he transgresses. (Bca 8.167)
Even if you are addressed in this way, if you will not do this, I shall subdue you alone; for all faults are dependent upon you.
"Where will you go, now that you have been seen by me? I shall destroy all your pride!
That was a different time in the past when you were able to destroy me."
Abandon now the hope that "I still have my own self-interest";
you have been sold by me to others, so do not think of your own great suffering.
If, indeed, out of negligence I do not give you over to sentient beings,
you will undoubtedly deliver me to the guardians of hell.
Having been thus harmed by you in many ways over a long period,
I shall now slay you, who act solely for your own self-interest, calling to mind those past enmities.
If you have affection for yourself, you should not take pleasure in [harming] yourself;
if this self is to be protected, it is not appropriate to protect it [by harming others].
Just as this body is provided with protection,
it becomes increasingly more delicate, and in that very same way, it inevitably falls [into ruin].
Even when he has fallen into such a state, this entire earth is not sufficient to fulfill his desire; who then will satisfy his longing?
For one who desires the impossible, suffering and the frustration of hope arise;
but for one who is free from hope in all things, prosperity never decays.
Therefore, one should not grant the body any scope for the increase of its desires;
for that object which is not grasped because it is desired is called "auspicious. (Bca 8.177)
This body ends in ashes, is motionless, and is moved by another;
it is a terrible vessel of impurity—why, then, do I have such attachment to it?
What use have I for this machine, whether it be alive or dead? What difference is there between it and a clod of earth? Alas! Why do you not abandon your egoism? (Bca 8.179)
Through partiality toward the body, suffering is acquired in vain;
what is the use of hatred or attachment toward this thing that is like a piece of wood? (Bca 8.180)
Whether it is thus protected by me or devoured by vultures and other scavengers, there is neither affection nor aversion; therefore, why do I feel attachment?
If he whom I provoke with anger and whom I please with honor does not himself know [the value of it], for whose sake is my exertion? (Bca 8.182)
Those who desire this body are indeed said to be my friends;
since everyone desires their own body, why are they not dear to me?
Therefore, disregarding my own interests, I have renounced my body for the welfare of the world;
hence, even though it is full of many defects, it is maintained like a vessel of karma.
Therefore, enough with the conduct of worldly people; remembering the discourse on heedfulness and warding off sloth and torpor, I shall follow the wise.
Therefore, in order to destroy the obscurations, I shall practice meditative concentration,
drawing the mind away from the wrong path and keeping it continuously fixed upon its own object.
In the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, the eighth chapter is the Perfection of Meditation.
Chapter Nine:
For the Sage taught this entire equipment for the sake of wisdom.
Therefore, one should generate wisdom out of a desire for the cessation of suffering.
The conventional and the ultimate—these are considered the two truths.
Reality is that which is beyond the scope of the intellect; the intellect is said to be the conventional.
In this regard, the world is seen to be twofold: the yogi and likewise the ordinary person.
Among these, the ordinary world is subverted by the world of the yogi.
Even yogins are surpassed by those who follow after them through their superior intellectual distinctions;
this is illustrated by an example accepted by both sides, for the sake of the task at hand, without further deliberation.
Entities are perceived by the world and are also conceptually constructed as being real;
however, there is no dispute between yogis and the world regarding the fact that they are like an illusion.
Even though form and so forth appear to perception, they are not established by means of valid cognition;
like the common consensus that there is purity in things such as the impure, that [perceptual appearance] is false.
And for the sake of leading people into the world [of the Dharma], entities were taught by the Protector;
in reality they are momentary, yet there is no contradiction with conventional truth.
There is no fault for those who see reality when they [employ] the conventional truth of yogis in relation to the world;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with worldly consensus in the case of describing a woman as impure.
How can there be merit from a Victor who is like an illusion, even if he exists in reality?
If a sentient being is like an illusion, how is it that they are born again after dying? (Bca 9.9)
As long as the collection of conditions exists, so long does illusion persist;
how can a sentient being exist in reality merely by virtue of a long continuum?
In cases such as the killing of an illusory person, there is no sin because of the absence of a [real] mind;
however, when the mind and illusion are conjoined, there arises both demerit and merit.
Because mantras and the like lack such power, a mind of illusion cannot arise;
furthermore, that various kinds of illusion arise from various conditions. (Bca 9.12)
Nowhere does a single condition possess the capacity for everything;
he who is extinguished in the ultimate sense might yet wander in cyclic existence through conventional reality.
If even a Buddha were to wander thus in cyclic existence, then what would be the use of the conduct of awakening?
For as long as conditions are not severed, even illusion is certainly not eliminated.
But because the conditions are severed, even conventionally there is no possibility [of its arising].
When even delusion does not exist, by what means is illusion perceived? (Bca 9.15)
When for you even illusion itself does not exist, then what is perceived?
Even if that form belongs to the mind alone, it does not exist in reality as something other [than the mind].
When the mind itself is an illusion, then what is seen by whom?
And it has been said by the Lord of the World: "The mind does not see the mind. (Bca 9.17)
Just as the edge of a sword does not cut itself, so too the mind [does not know itself];
and just as a lamp illuminates its own form, [so does the mind]. If this is argued: Bca_9.18.
A lamp is not illuminated at all because it is not enveloped by darkness;
for a crystal is not blue [by nature], nor does it depend on anything else for its blueness.
Likewise, some things are seen to depend on others while others are independent;
[if it were not blue], that which is not blue could not by itself make itself blue. (Bca 9.20)
For if it is already blue, who could make itself blue by itself?
If it is not blue, it could not make itself blue by itself.
Having known that "the lamp shines," it is spoken by means of knowledge;
but having known that "the intellect shines," by whom is this spoken?
Whether manifest or unmanifest, when it is not perceived by anyone,
it is as futile as describing the playful dance of the daughter of a barren woman.
If self-awareness does not exist, how can consciousness be remembered?
Memory arises from a connection with what was experienced by another, just like the poison of a rat.
Because it is seen when conjoined with other conditions, it is itself that which shines forth;
a jar seen through the application of a magical ointment does not become the ointment itself.
What is seen, heard, or known is not here prohibited;
rather, it is the conceptualization of these as real that is prevented here, for it is the cause of suffering.
If it is conceived that illusion is neither other than the mind nor non-other than it—if it were a real entity, how could it not be other? And if it is non-other, it does not exist as a real entity.
Just as an illusion is seen even though it does not exist, so too is the mind the seer.
If cyclic existence were based on a real entity, it would be otherwise, like space.
How could non-existence possess activity by depending on a real entity?
For, according to you, the mind would then become solitary, lacking any companion.
When the mind is freed from the graspable, then all are Tathāgatas. And what benefit is gained by merely imagining "mind-only" in this way? (Bca 9.30)
Even when things are known to be like an illusion, how is affliction removed? For even the creator of an illusory woman may still give rise to passion for her. (Bca 9.31)
For the latent impression of the afflictions regarding the objects of knowledge has not been abandoned by the one who performs that [meditation];
therefore, at the time of that [false] view, his impression of emptiness is weak. (Bca 9.32)
By cultivating the impression of emptiness, the impression of existence is discarded;
and by practicing the realization that "nothing exists," even that [impression] is later abandoned.
When no entity is found that could be conceptualized as "non-existent," then how could non-existence,
being without a basis, appear before the mind?
When neither existence nor non-existence presents itself before the mind, then,
due to the absence of any other alternative, it becomes supportless and is stilled.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-granting tree fulfill one's desires,
so too is the form of the Victor perceived through the power of those to be trained and his own former aspirations.
Just as a snake-charmer, having empowered a ritual pillar, passes away; even long after he has perished, that pillar continues to neutralize poisons and the like. (Bca 9.37)
In accordance with his conduct of awakening, even the pillar of the Victor accomplishes all tasks, even when the Bodhisattva has passed into nirvāṇa.
How can an offering made to one who is without mind be fruitful?
For it is taught that [the merit] is exactly the same for one who is living and for one who has entered nirvāṇa. (Bca 9.39)

Furthermore, how is it that an offering made to a Buddha who exists either conventionally or in reality bears fruit? It is because of scripture (*āgama*). Just as [it is said]: "An offering made to a true Buddha is fruitful. (Bca 9.40)
Liberation comes from seeing the truth; what is the use of seeing emptiness?
For there is a scriptural tradition stating that enlightenment is not attained without this path.
"Now, the Mahāyāna is unestablished; how then is your scripture established?
Since that [Mahāyāna] is established for both [parties], it was not established for you from the very beginning."
Whatever basis for confidence you have in that [Veda], apply it to the Mahāyāna as well;
otherwise, if both were equally accepted as true, then the Vedas and so forth would also possess truth.
If you say that the Mahāyāna is subject to dispute, then abandon your own scripture as well,
for it is disputed by non-Buddhists, and other scriptures are disputed by your own and by others alike.
The teaching has the state of being a monk as its root, yet even that state of being a monk is suffering for those whose minds possess objective referents; even nirvana remains unstable for them.
If liberation results from the abandonment of the afflictions, let it occur immediately thereafter;
for the efficacy of karma is observed even in one who is free from afflictions.
If it is considered that craving does not constitute grasping, then why does this craving—which exists like their delusion—not exist for them even when it is non-afflicted? (Bca 9.47)
Craving has feeling as its condition, and these [beings] possess feelings;
therefore, one should abide with a mind that has an object of focus, wherever that may be.
Without emptiness, the mind arises again in bondage, as in the attainment of non-perception; therefore, one should cultivate emptiness.
If a statement is accepted as the word of the Buddha because it appears in a sūtra,
why do you not consider the Mahāyāna to be essentially identical to your own sūtras?
If everything were faulty because of a single [text] that is not being accepted,
then why is everything spoken by the Victor not [accepted] simply because of one [text] that is equal to a Sūtra?
That which cannot be fathomed even by the foremost disciples headed by Mahākāśyapa—who would make it graspable because you have not understood it? (Bca 9.52)
Through fear of attachment, one fails to attain liberation, and thus stability remains within cyclic existence;
this is the fruit of emptiness for the sake of those who suffer due to delusion.
Thus, in this way, a refutation against the position of emptiness is not tenable;
therefore, one should cultivate emptiness without any doubt.
For emptiness is the antidote to the darkness of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations;
why, then, does one who desires swift omniscience not cultivate it? (Bca 9.55)
Since fear arises from that thing which produces suffering,
and emptiness is the pacifier of suffering, why then does fear arise from it?
If there were some "I" whatsoever, then fear might arise from this or that;
but if I myself am nothing at all, for whom will there be fear?
I am not the teeth, hair, or nails; I am not the bone, nor am I the blood; I am not the snot, nor the phlegm, nor the pus, nor even the lymph.
I am not the fat, nor the sweat, nor the marrow, nor the entrails;
I am not the small intestine, nor the large intestine, nor feces and urine.
I am not flesh, nor sinew, nor heat, nor am I wind;
I am not the cavities, nor in any way the six consciousnesses.
If that [cognition] were the knowledge of sound, then sound would be perceived at all times;
but what does it know without an object of knowledge (jñeya), by virtue of which it is designated as "knowledge"? (Bca 9.61)
If knowledge were to exist in one who is unaware, it would follow that even a piece of wood possesses knowledge;
therefore, it is certain that there is no knowledge in the absence of an object of knowledge.
If it knows that very form, why does it not hear [sound] as well?
If you say it is because of the absence of sound, then that cognition [of form] would also be non-existent.
How can that which has the nature of perceiving sound be the perception of form?
A single entity is designated as both father and son, but not in reality.
Since neither the son nor the father consists of sattva, rajas, or tamas,
their inherent nature (svabhāva) as being engaged in the apprehension of sound is not perceived.
If that very same [person] exists in another form like an actor, he too is impermanent;
if it were the case that he himself possesses a different intrinsic nature, then this would be a novel kind of identity.
If that other form is unreal, let its own true nature be stated.
If it is said to be consciousness, then it follows that all persons are one.
When there is a unity between the sentient and the insentient because their existence is equal,
and when the distinction between them is false, then what could be the basis for their similarity?
And I am certainly not insentient, because I lack sentience, like a cloth or similar objects.
If, on the other hand, I were a knower through association with consciousness, it would follow that when I am ignorant, I am destroyed.
If the self remains entirely unmodified, what has consciousness done for it?
Thus, the selfhood of one who is ignorant and inactive is considered to be like that of space.
If the connection between action and its fruit is not tenable without a self,
then once the agent has perished after performing the action, to whom will the fruit belong?
Since the fruits of action for both of us are established as having distinct substrates,
and since the self therein is devoid of activity, is not this debate indeed futile?
It is not possible for one who possesses a cause to be joined with its fruit;
it is taught that there is an agent and an enjoyer by relying on the unity of the continuum.
The past and future mind are not "I," for they do not exist;
and the mind that has arisen is "I," but once it has perished, "I" no longer exist. (Bca 9.74)
Just as the trunk of a plantain tree, when dissected part by part, is nothing at all,
so too am I non-existent when sought through analytical investigation.
If it is argued, "If a sentient being does not exist, for whom is there compassion?", [the answer is:
it is for that which is imagined through delusion by one who has undertaken [this practice] for the sake of the task to be accomplished.
If there were no sentient being, whose would be the task? Yet this striving is indeed born of delusion;
however, the delusion regarding the task undertaken for the sake of pacifying suffering is not to be obstructed.
The ego-sense is the cause of suffering, and it increases due to delusion regarding a self;
if it cannot be turned back even from that, then the cultivation of selflessness is better.
The body is not the feet, nor the shanks, nor the thighs;
the body is not the hips, nor the belly, nor is it the back, nor the chest, nor even the arms.
There are no hands, nor these sides, nor the armpits, nor the characteristics of the shoulders;
there is no neck, nor the head—then what, indeed, is the body here?
If this body exists in all [parts] only by way of one part, then the parts exist within their own parts; where, then, does it itself abide?
If the body were present in its entirety in every part, such as the hands and so forth,
then there would be as many bodies as there are those hands and other parts.
The body is neither within nor without; how then can there be a body in the hands and other limbs?
Since it does not exist separately from the hands and so forth, how indeed does it exist at all?

That body does not exist; rather, it is through delusion that the notion of a "body" arises with respect to the hands and so forth, just as the notion of a "man" arises toward a phallus due to its particular configuration.
As long as the collection of conditions exists, so long does the body appear like a person;
likewise, as long as that collection exists in the hands and other limbs, so long is the body perceived there.
In this way, because it is a collection of fingers, what would the foot be?
That too, being a collection of joints, and the joint as well, through the division of its own parts.
Even parts are divided by atoms, and even that atom is [divided] according to the divisions of space;
since the divisions of space lack parts, there is no atom, and therefore no such thing as space exists.
Thus, what discerning person would be attached to form, which is like a dream?
Since the body itself does not exist in this way, who then is a woman and who is a man?
If suffering exists in reality, why does it not afflict those who are intensely joyful?
And if things such as delicacies constitute happiness for one afflicted by grief and the like, why do they not please them?
If that [feeling] is not experienced because it is overwhelmed by something more powerful,
how can it possess the nature of feeling when its essence is not experience?
Surely its grossness has been removed by its subtlety;
if there should be yet another degree of satisfaction, then that too is its subtlety.
If suffering does not arise when a contrary cognition occurs,
then has it not indeed followed that feeling is merely an adherence to conceptual construction?
For this very reason, this investigation is cultivated as its antidote;
for yogins have meditation born from the field of conceptual construction as their sustenance.
If the sense faculty and its object are separated by an interval, how could there be contact between them?
Even if they were without an interval, how could they be one; what could possibly have conjunction with what?
One atom cannot enter another atom, for it is devoid of space and equal in size;
in the absence of entry, there can be no mingling, and in the absence of mingling, there is no conjunction.
And how indeed can conjunction be possible for that which is partless?
If you have seen conjunction in something partless, show it to us.
But for consciousness, which is formless, conjunction is not at all possible; nor is it possible for an aggregate, because—as was previously analyzed—it lacks substantial reality.
Thus, in the absence of contact, how could there be the arising of sensation?
For what purpose is this exertion? To whom would there be affliction, and from what would it arise?
When there is no experiencer whatsoever and feeling does not exist,
then having seen this state, O craving, why do you not shatter?
It is seen and even touched by the mind, which is like a dream or an illusion;
because it arises simultaneously with that mind, feeling is not perceived as a separate entity.
That which has arisen both before and after is remembered, not experienced;
it does not experience itself, nor is it experienced by another.
There is no experiencer whatsoever apart from the sensation itself; thus, in reality, when this collection is devoid of self, who indeed is afflicted by it?
The mind does not abide in the sense faculties, nor in forms and so forth, nor in between them;
the mind is found neither within, nor without, nor anywhere else.
That which is neither in the body nor elsewhere, neither mixed nor separate anywhere—that is nothing at all; therefore, sentient beings are by nature in a state of final nirvana.
If cognition exists prior to the object of knowledge, upon what could it depend for its arising?
If cognition exists simultaneously with the object of knowledge, upon what could it depend for its arising?
If, on the other hand, knowledge were to arise after the object of knowledge, then from what would that knowledge itself arise?
In this way, the arising of all phenomena is not established.
If conventional reality does not exist in this way, then from where would the two truths arise?
Or, if it were to exist through another conventional reality, how could a sentient being ever attain liberation?
This is a conceptual construction of another's mind; however, by one's own conventional perspective, it does not exist.
That [mind] is later determined to exist; if it did not exist, then conventional reality itself would not exist.
Conceptual construction and the conceptually constructed—these two are mutually dependent;
all investigation is said to proceed by relying on what is conventionally established.
But when that very investigation is itself investigated by another investigation,
then there is an infinite regress, because that investigation too must be investigated.
But when the object of investigation has been investigated, there is no basis for further investigation;
because it lacks a basis, it does not arise, and that is called nirvāṇa.
But for one for whom both of these are real, that person is in an extremely precarious state:
if the object exists by virtue of cognition, then what is the status of the existence of the cognition itself?
Now, if knowledge exists by virtue of the object of knowledge, what is the status of the existence of that object?
Or, if they exist by virtue of each other, both would necessarily be non-existent.
If there is no father without a son, how can there be the birth of a son?
In the absence of a son, there is no father; likewise, the reality of both of them [is non-existent].
A sprout arises from a seed, and by that very [sprout] the seed is indicated;
why then is the existence of that [seed] not understood through the knowledge produced from the object of knowledge?
From the knowledge that the sprout exists, it is understood that the seed exists;
but from where is the existence of that knowledge itself known, by which the object of knowledge is apprehended? (Bca 9.116)
The world, for its part, perceives through direct observation that everything depends upon a cause;
indeed, the various distinctions among lotuses, stalks, and so forth arise from a distinction in their causes.
If it is asked what causes the distinction between causes, it is due to the differentiation of prior causes.
And if it is asked why a cause yields its fruit, it is through the power of prior causes.
If you claim that God is the cause of the world, tell me first: who is this God?
If it is the elements, let it be so; what is the point of such exertion over a mere name?
Moreover, earth and the other elements are manifold, impermanent, devoid of activity, and not deities; they are to be transgressed and are impure—therefore, they are not the Lord.
Space is not the Lord because it is inactive; nor is the self, due to its prior refutation.
Furthermore, how can it be said that the agency of the inconceivable is itself inconceivable?
What does he wish to create by that? If it is the self, surely that is eternal;
likewise, the earth and other elements, the Lord, knowledge, and the beginningless object of knowledge [are all eternal]. (Bca 9.122)
Tell me, what is produced by karma other than pleasure and pain?
If there is no beginning to the cause, how could there be a beginning to the fruit?
Why does it not act at all times? For it does not depend on anything else;
since there is nothing else uncreated by it, what could it possibly depend upon? (Bca 9.124)
If the cause depends upon a collection of conditions, then God does not;
for He is not able to act when the collection is present, nor is He able to act in its absence.
If the Lord acts without desire, it follows that he is dependent on something else;
even if he acts with desire, he would be dependent on that desire. For one who acts in this way, how can there be lordship?
Those who assert that atoms are eternal have also been refuted previously.
The Sāṃkhyas, however, maintain that *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is the eternal cause of the world.
The qualities known as sattva, rajas, and tamas, when existing in equilibrium, are called *pradhāna*; when they are in disequilibrium, they are said to be the world.
It is illogical for a single entity to possess three natures; therefore, that [triple nature] does not exist.
Likewise, the qualities do not exist, for they too are each threefold.
Furthermore, in the absence of qualities, the existence of sound and so forth is extremely remote;
and since cloth and such things are insentient, pleasure and the like are impossible therein as well.
If you claim that entities have that [pleasure, etc. as their cause, then surely those entities have already been analyzed.
Furthermore, pleasure and so forth alone are the causes; cloth and such things do not arise from them.
Pleasure and so forth would belong to the cloth and other objects; in the absence of those [objects], pleasure and so forth do not exist.
Furthermore, the permanence of pleasure and so forth is never perceived at any time.
If the manifestation of pleasure truly exists, why is it not perceived?
That very same [pleasure] becomes subtle; how can that which is gross also be subtle? (Bca 9.133)
Having abandoned grossness, it becomes subtle; since grossness and subtlety are impermanent, why is impermanence not likewise accepted for every object? (Bca 9.134)
If grossness is not distinct from pleasure, then the impermanence of pleasure is evident.
If it is thought that "nothing arises from non-existence because of its lack of being," [that is incorrect].
The production of a manifest effect from what is non-existent is established for you even against your will;
if the fruit were already present in the cause, then one who eats food would be eating filth.
One should buy cotton seeds with the very price intended for cloth and wear them;
if the world does not see this due to delusion, such is the situation even for one who knows the truth.
The world also possesses that same cognition; why then does it not see [the truth]?
If you argue that the world is not an authority, then even clear perception would be non-existent.
If a valid means of cognition were invalid, then that which was cognized by it would indeed be false;
consequently, emptiness in its true sense would not be established for entities.
Without contacting an imagined entity, its non-existence cannot be apprehended;
therefore, since the entity is false, its non-existence is clearly false as well.
Therefore, when a son is lost in a dream, the conceptualization that "he does not exist" obstructs the arising of the conceptualization of his existence; and that [conceptualization] is false.
Therefore, through such investigation, nothing exists without a cause,
nor is anything established within conditions, whether taken individually or collectively.
It has not come from anywhere else, nor does it stay, nor does it go;
what difference is there between this and an illusion, that fools have treated it as real? (Bca 9.143)
That which is created by illusion and that which is produced by causes—from where does it come, and to where does it go? Let this be investigated. (Bca 9.144)
That which is seen due to the proximity of another is not seen because of its absence;
since it is artificial and like a reflection, how can there be reality in it?
What is the use of a cause for an entity that already exists?
And what is the use of a cause for one that does not exist? (Bca 9.146)
There is no transformation of a non-entity even by means of hundreds of millions of causes;
how then could an entity remain in that same state, or what else could have attained the nature of an entity?
If there is no existence at the time of non-existence, when will existence ever come to be?
For that non-existence cannot be dispelled by an existence that has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, as long as non-existence has not departed, there is no possibility for existence to arise;
nor does existence ever attain the state of non-existence, for that would entail the consequence of having two natures.
And thus there is no contradiction, nor does any entity exist at any time;
therefore, this entire world is unborn and unceasing.
The realms of existence are like dreams when investigated; they are like plantain trees.
In reality, there is no difference between those who have attained liberation and those who have not.
Thus, when all phenomena are empty, what could be gained and what could be lost?
Who could be honored or insulted, and who could come into being?
Whence comes pleasure or pain? What is dear and what is not dear?
What is craving, and where is that craving when sought by its own nature?
Upon reflection, who is this world of living beings? Who indeed here will die? Who will come to be, who has been, who is a kinsman, and who is whose friend? (Bca 9.154)
Let those like me grasp everything as being like space;
for people become angry or delighted due to the causes of quarrels and festivals.
Desiring happiness for themselves, they pass their time with great difficulty through sorrows, anxieties, despondencies, and mutual wounding and piercing, all due to their sinful deeds.
Having died, they fall into states of woe characterized by long and intense suffering;
yet, having repeatedly returned to happy rebirths and having repeatedly become accustomed to happiness, [they fall again].
In cyclic existence there are many precipices, and therein such non-existence;
therein there is mutual contradiction, and therein no such reality would exist.
And therein lie incomparable, intense oceans of endless suffering;
likewise, there is a lack of strength, and even there, the lifespan is brief.
Even there, one is beset by the activities for livelihood and health, by hunger, exhaustion,
and fatigue, by sleep, by afflictions, and likewise by fruitless association with the foolish.

Life passes away swiftly and in vain, yet discernment is extremely difficult to find; even when that is attained, how can there be the capacity to ward off the distractions one has long practiced? (Bca 9.161)
Even there, Māra strives to cast one down into the great abysses of the miserable realms;
furthermore, because of the abundance of false paths there, doubt is difficult to overcome.

Furthermore, the rarity of a favorable moment, the extreme difficulty of a Buddha’s appearance, and the flood of afflictions that is hard to restrain—alas, what a succession of sufferings! (Bca 9.163)
"Alas! How truly pitiable are these who dwell in a flood of suffering;
though they are thus exceedingly ill-situated, they do not perceive their own wretched condition. (Bca 9.164)
Just as someone who has bathed again and again might repeatedly enter the fire,
so too do those who are in extreme misery consider themselves to be in a state of well-being.
For those who thus sport as if they were ageless and immortal, while living in this manner,
terrible calamities will arrive, having placed death right before them.
When shall I bring peace to those scorched by the fire of suffering,
using my own provisions for happiness produced from the clouds of merit?
When, through the non-apprehension of conventional reality, shall I respectfully teach emptiness to those who hold the view of apprehension, so that they may gather the equipment of merit?
The ninth chapter, titled "The Perfection of Wisdom," from the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
Whatever merit I have gained by reflecting upon this *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, [may it lead all beings to the state of omniscience].
By this, may all people be adorned with the conduct of awakening.
May all those in every direction who are afflicted by physical and mental suffering obtain oceans of happiness and joy through my merits.
"May there never be a loss of happiness for them as long as saṃsāra lasts; may the world incessantly attain the bliss of a bodhisattva. (Bca 10.3)
May as many beings as there are in the hells throughout all world-systems rejoice in Sukhāvatī through the fragrances of bliss.
May those afflicted by cold obtain warmth, and may those afflicted by heat become cool,
through oceans of water produced from the great clouds of the Bodhisattvas.
May the Forest of Sword-Leaves for them have the splendor of the Nandana Grove;
and may the thorny Śālmalī trees become wish-fulfilling trees.

May the regions of hell become heart-pleasing with lakes whose beauty is delightful with the clamor of gallinules, ducks, ruddy geese, swans, and the like, and which possess the fragrance of lotuses grown through great effort.
May that heap of coals become a heap of jewels, and may the heated earth become a floor of crystal;
may the mountains of the world-system become celestial palaces for worship, filled with Sugatas.
From this day forward, let there be a rain of flowers instead of the rain of burning coals, heated stones, and weapons;
and let that mutual battle with weapons henceforth be a flower-battle for the sake of play.

May those whose flesh has fallen away, whose bodies consist only of bones white as jasmine, and who were submerged in the Vaitaraṇī river whose waters are like fire, obtain divine forms through the power of my merit; and together with celestial nymphs, may they dwell upon the Mandākinī.

Terrified, let the messengers of Yama, the crows, the vultures, and the other horrors here suddenly behold [this light]! "Whose gentle radiance is this, producing happiness and joy, by which the darkness has been destroyed on all sides?
Thus looking upward and seeing Vajrapāṇi blazing in the expanse of the sky, let them, their misdeeds dispelled by the force of their joy, go forth together with him.

May a rain of lotuses mixed with fragrant water fall, seen extinguishing the fires of hell with the sound "sham"; what is this?—it is called "delight" born of happiness; why should there not be a vision of the Lotus-Handed One for the denizens of hell? (Bca 10.12)
"Come, come quickly! O brothers, dispel our fear! We have been restored to life; here has arrived for us some young *cīrin* who bestows blazing fearlessness.

Through his majestic power, all calamity has vanished, floods of joy have arisen, the mind of awakening (*saṃbodhicitta*) has been born, and compassion—the mother who protects all beings—has appeared. (Bca 10.13)
Behold him, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the crowns of hundreds of gods, his gaze moist with compassion as a rain of many flowers falls upon his head;

seeing Mañjughoṣa before them, praised by delightful gabled palaces and accompanied by the songs of thousands of celestial women singing hymns—let there now be a tumultuous roar from the denizens of hell!

Thus, by means of my merits, may those beings in the hells rejoice upon beholding clouds of Bodhisattvas headed by Samantabhadra, accompanied by rains and breezes that are pleasant, cool, and fragrant. (Bca 10.15)
May the intense sufferings and the fears of the hell-beings be stilled;
may all those dwelling in the miserable realms be liberated from those states of woe.
May the fear of devouring one another depart from the animals;
may the hungry ghosts become happy, like the humans of Uttarakuru.
May the *pretas* be fully satiated, bathed,
and forever cooled by the streams of milk flowing from the hands of the noble Avalokiteśvara.
May the blind see forms, and may the deaf always hear.
And may pregnant women give birth without pain, like Queen Māyā.
May they obtain clothing, food, drink, garlands, sandalwood, ornaments,
and everything their hearts desire— all that is conducive to their welfare.
May those who are afraid be fearless; may those afflicted by sorrow obtain joy;
and may those who are anxious become free from anxiety and possessed of steadfastness.
May those who are sick attain health; may all be released from every bond;
may the weak become strong, and may they be affectionate toward one another.
May all directions be auspicious for everyone traveling on the road;
may whatever purpose they go to fulfill be accomplished by the appropriate means.
May those embarked upon voyages by ship have their desires fulfilled;
having reached the shore in safety, may they rejoice together with their kinsmen.
May those who have strayed onto wrong paths in the wilderness find a caravan;
and may they travel without fatigue, free from fear of thieves, tigers, and other dangers.
May the deities provide protection for those who are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless; for those in danger from disease, wild forests, and the like; and for the helpless, the young, and the elderly.
May they be forever free from all unfavorable conditions, endowed with faith, wisdom, and compassion,
perfected in appearance and conduct, and always possessed of the memory of their past lives.
May they possess inexhaustible treasuries as vast as the mountain mines,
free from conflict and free from hardship, with their livelihoods under their own control.
May those beings who possess little splendor become possessed of great splendor;
may those ascetics who are deformed become endowed with perfect beauty.
Whatever women there may be in the world, let them attain manhood;
and let those base ones obtain that [state], and let their pride be destroyed.
By this merit of mine, may all sentient beings without exception,
having desisted from all misdeeds, always perform what is wholesome.
Unseparated from the thought of awakening, devoted to the conduct of awakening,
they are embraced by the Buddhas and remain free from the deeds of Māra.
May all those sentient beings have immeasurable lifespans;
may they always live in happiness, and may even the word "death" perish.
May all directions become delightful with groves of wish-fulfilling trees,
filled with Buddhas and their sons, enchanting with the sounds of the Dharma.
May the ground everywhere be free from gravel and the like, level as the palm of a hand, soft, and made of lapis lazuli.
May the great assemblies of Bodhisattvas sit all around and adorn the surface of the earth with their own splendors.
Let the sound of the Dharma be heard without ceasing by all embodied beings—from the birds, from all the trees, from the rays of light, and even from the sky. (Bca 10.37)
May they always attain union with the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas,
and may they worship the Teacher of the World with infinite clouds of offerings.
May the god send rain in due season, may there be an abundance of crops,
may the world be prosperous, and may the king be righteous.
May medicinal herbs be effective; may the mantras succeed for those who recite them;
and may the ḍākinīs, rākṣasas, and others be filled with compassion.
May no sentient being be suffering, may none be sinful, and may none be diseased;
may none be inferior or despised, and may no one be dejected in mind.
May the monasteries be well-established, filled with the recitation and study of the scriptures;
may there always be harmony within the Saṅgha, and may the work of the Saṅgha be accomplished.
May the monks who have attained discernment and desire the training meditate with pliant minds, free from all distractions.
May the bhikṣuṇīs be successful and free from quarrels and weariness;
likewise, may all those who have gone forth possess unimpaired ethical discipline.
May those of immoral conduct be filled with spiritual urgency and always delight in the destruction of evil;
may they attain a happy rebirth and there maintain their vows without violation.
May the wise be honored; may those who live on alms-food receive their sustenance;
may they possess pure mental continuums and have their fame celebrated in all directions.
Without experiencing the suffering of the lower realms and without undergoing difficult ascetic practices,
may all beings attain Buddhahood with a single divine body.
May all the perfectly awakened Buddhas be worshipped in manifold ways by all sentient beings;
may they be exceedingly happy with the inconceivable bliss of a Buddha.
May the aspirations of the Bodhisattvas for the sake of the world be fulfilled;
may whatever those Protectors intend for sentient beings come to fruition.
May the Pratyekabuddhas and likewise the Śrāvakas be happy,
being constantly honored with reverence by gods, asuras, and humans.
Through the protection of Mañjughoṣa, may I always attain the recollection of past lives and the state of renunciation, until I reach the Stage of Joy.
May I sustain myself with whatever seat [or food] is available, endowed with strength,
and may I obtain the necessary conditions for dwelling in solitude throughout all my births.
And whenever I should desire to see or wish to ask anything,
may I behold that very Protector, Mañjunātha, without any obstacle.
In accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings throughout the expanse of the ten directions,
whatever Mañjuśrī practices, may that very conduct be mine as well.
As long as space endures,
and as long as the world endures, may I remain, destroying the sufferings of the world.
Whatever suffering there is in the world, may it all ripen upon me;
and by all the virtues of the Bodhisattvas, may the world be happy.
May the Teaching— the sole medicine for the suffering of the world, the source of all prosperity and happiness— endure for a long time, accompanied by gain and honor.
I pay homage to Mañjughoṣa, by whose grace my mind is directed toward what is auspicious;
I revere the spiritual friend, by whose grace it increases. (Bca 10.58)
The tenth chapter of the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, titled "Dedication."
